# 2.2 Properties of Water

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Polarity

Water's **polarity** means there is a **greater probability of finding its shared electrons closer to its oxygen atom**.

**Polar molecules have unevenly distributed charges** — **oxygen is slightly negative, hydrogen slightly positive**.

## Hydrogen bonding

A **hydrogen bond** is a **weak intermolecular attraction between hydrogen on one molecule and oxygen on another**.

## Cohesion, adhesion, and capillary action

| Property | Definition | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the **same** substance | Causes **surface tension** |
| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of **different** substances | Causes **menisci** to form |

**Capillary action** works by both at once: **cohesion holds the continuous column of water together as adhesion causes it to rise**. This is what **draws water out of roots into stems**.

## Solutions

Water's polarity lets it **dissolve ionic compounds and other polar molecules**.

- **Solute** — the substance that is dissolved
- **Solvent** — the substance in which the solute dissolves

## The pH scale

The **pH scale** measures the **concentration of H⁺ ions** in a solution, ranging from **0 (very acidic) to 14 (very basic)**.

| pH | Condition | Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| **< 7** | Acidic | [H⁺] > [OH⁻] |
| **= 7** | Neutral | [H⁺] = [OH⁻] |
| **> 7** | Basic | [H⁺] < [OH⁻] |

$$\text{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^+}], \qquad [\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$$

Because the scale is **logarithmic**, each whole step is a **tenfold** change in H⁺ concentration — pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5, not slightly more.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polarity** | The greater probability of finding water's shared electrons closer to its oxygen atom |
| **Polar molecule** | A molecule with unevenly distributed charges |
| **Hydrogen bond** | A weak intermolecular attraction between hydrogen on one molecule and oxygen on another |
| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the same substance, causing surface tension |
| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of different substances, causing menisci |
| **Capillary action** | Cohesion holding a water column together while adhesion causes it to rise |
| **Solute** | The substance that is dissolved |
| **Solvent** | The substance in which the solute dissolves |
| **pH scale** | A logarithmic measure of H⁺ concentration, from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very basic) |

# 3.1 What Is Ecology?

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The basics

The **biosphere** consists of **all life and all parts of the Earth with life**.

**Ecology** is the **scientific study of interactions among organisms, and between organisms and their physical environment**.

The Greek root is **oikos**, meaning *house*:

- **Ecology** — the study of nature's "houses" and the inhabitants of those houses
- **Economics** — the study of human "houses" and interactions involving money and trade

The shared root is not a coincidence, and it is a useful reminder of what ecology studies: not organisms alone but the **household they run**.

## Levels of organisation

From least to most inclusive:

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1. Individual organism** | A single living thing |
| **2. Population** | A group of individuals of **one species** living in the **same area**. A **species** is a group of similar organisms that can produce **fertile offspring** |
| **3. Community** | **All the different populations** that live together in an area |
| **4. Ecosystem** | All organisms in an area **together with their physical environment** |
| **5. Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing **similar climates and organisms** |
| **6. Biosphere** | Our entire planet |

## Environmental factors

The **environment** is **all the conditions and factors surrounding an organism**.

| Factor | Nature | Definition | Example (for a bullfrog) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Biotic** | Biological | Any **living** part of the environment an organism might interact with | Insects and herons |
| **Abiotic** | Physical | Any **nonliving** part of the environment | Water availability and temperature |

**Both types of factor can influence the other**, shaping an environment with their dynamic mix.

## Ecological methods

- **Observation**
- **Experimentation** — can be used to **test hypotheses**
- **Modelling** — helps understand events that happen over **long periods of time or large distances**, using **formulas based on data from observation and experimentation**

Note why modelling exists as a third method: some ecological questions span centuries or continents, where neither watching nor experimenting is possible.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biosphere** | All life and all parts of the Earth with life |
| **Ecology** | The scientific study of interactions among organisms and with their physical environment |
| **Population** | A group of individuals of one species living in the same area |
| **Species** | Similar organisms that can produce fertile offspring |
| **Community** | All the different populations living together in an area |
| **Ecosystem** | All organisms in an area together with their physical environment |
| **Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing similar climates and organisms |
| **Environment** | All conditions and factors surrounding an organism |
| **Biotic factor** | Any living part of the environment an organism might interact with |
| **Abiotic factor** | Any nonliving part of the environment |
| **Modelling** | Using formulas based on observational and experimental data to understand events over long times or distances |

# 3.2 Energy, Producers, and Consumers

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Producers

**Autotrophs** are organisms that **use solar or chemical energy to produce "food" (glucose)**.

They are also called **primary producers**, because they are the **first producers of energy-rich compounds** later used by other organisms, and they are **essential to energy flow in the biosphere**.

The Greek roots are **auto** (by itself) and **trophikos** (to feed).

### Photosynthesis

A process in which **light energy powers reactions to produce carbohydrates**, converting **carbon dioxide and water into oxygen and energy-rich sugars and starches**.

Performed by:

- **Plants**, on land
- **Algae**, in freshwater and the upper layers of the ocean
- **Bacteria** (commonly **cyanobacteria**), in tidal flats and salt marshes

### Chemosynthesis

A process in which **chemical energy is used to produce carbohydrates**. **Chemosynthetic bacteria power ecosystems** at deep-sea volcanic vents, hot springs, and coastal tidal marshes.

## Consumers

**Heterotrophs** must **acquire energy and nutrients from other organisms**.

| Type | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Carnivores** | Kill and eat other animals | Snakes, dogs, cats |
| **Herbivores** | Eat plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits | Cows, caterpillars, deer |
| **Omnivores** | Diets include both plants and animals | Humans, bears, pigs |
| **Scavengers** | Consume carcasses of animals killed by other predators or dead by other means | Vultures, flies |
| **Decomposers (saprotrophs)** | Release digestive enzymes to break down organic matter **externally**, producing **detritus** | Fungi, bacteria |
| **Detritivores** | Feed on **detritus particles**, chewing and grinding them into smaller pieces; commonly digest the decomposers living on or in those particles | Mites, snails, shrimp, crabs |

**Detritus** is small pieces of dead and decaying plant and animal remains.

Note the trade-off in carnivory: **catching and killing prey requires energy**, but meat is generally **rich in nutrients and energy and easily digested**.

## Beyond the consumer categories

**Strict categories do not represent the full complexity.**

- **Plant leaves are much less nutritious and harder to digest than seeds or fruits**, so herbivores that eat different parts differ in how they obtain and digest food. **Most birds do not have the digestive systems to digest leaves**
- **Hyenas**, though classified as carnivores, **will scavenge**
- **Aquatic animals** eat a mixture of algae, bits of animal carcasses, and detritus
- **Carnivorous plants and euglenoids are mixotrophic** — both heterotrophic and autotrophic

This is the section's real point: the categories are a useful first pass, and almost every organism examined closely violates them somewhere.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Autotroph** | An organism using solar or chemical energy to produce food (glucose) |
| **Primary producer** | Another name for an autotroph — the first producer of energy-rich compounds |
| **Photosynthesis** | Light energy powering reactions that convert CO₂ and water into oxygen and sugars |
| **Chemosynthesis** | Chemical energy being used to produce carbohydrates |
| **Heterotroph** | An organism that must acquire energy and nutrients from other organisms |
| **Carnivore** | A consumer that kills and eats other animals |
| **Herbivore** | A consumer that eats plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits |
| **Omnivore** | A consumer whose diet includes both plants and animals |
| **Scavenger** | A consumer of carcasses killed by others or dead by other means |
| **Decomposer (saprotroph)** | An organism releasing digestive enzymes to break down organic matter externally |
| **Detritus** | Small pieces of dead and decaying plant and animal remains |
| **Detritivore** | An organism feeding on detritus particles, grinding them smaller |
| **Mixotroph** | An organism that is both heterotrophic and autotrophic |

# 3.3 Energy Flow in Ecosystems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Food chains and food webs

A **food chain** is **a series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by eating and being eaten**. **Energy flows through an ecosystem in a one-way stream.**

An example, four steps from producer to top predator:

$$\text{algae (phytoplankton)} \rightarrow \text{krill (zooplankton)} \rightarrow \text{penguin} \rightarrow \text{seal} \rightarrow \text{orca}$$

**Plankton** are small aquatic floating organisms. The **orca** is the top predator here, **four steps removed from the producer**.

A **food web** is **a network of feeding interactions, representing interconnected food chains** — necessary because **many animals eat more than one kind of food**.

**Decomposers in food webs recycle nutrients**, releasing them for primary producers to use. **A change in the population of one species can disturb other organisms in the web.**

## Ecological pyramids

A **trophic level** is **each step in a food chain or food web** — primary producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer.

**Ecological pyramids** show the **relative amount of certain things at each trophic level** in an ecosystem.

### Pyramid of energy

Shows the **relative amount of energy available at each level**, in **kJ · m⁻² · y⁻¹**.

**About 10 percent of the energy in one trophic level is transferred to the next.** The other **90 percent is lost** as heat, and as non-ingested or non-digested parts.

### Pyramid of biomass

Shows the **relative amount of living organic matter at each level**, in **g · m⁻²**.

**It can be an inverted triangle when:**

- **In winter**, producers die or lose leaf mass while consumers retain stored mass
- **In the deep sea**, with huge top predators (whales, giant squid) and producers that come and go quickly

### Pyramid of numbers

Shows the **relative number of living organisms at each level**.

**It can be inverted when consumers are much less massive than their food sources** — thousands of insects grazing on a single tree.

The inversions are the point worth holding onto. **A pyramid of energy can never be inverted**, because energy is always lost between levels; biomass and numbers can invert, because they measure standing stock at one moment rather than flow.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Food chain** | A series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by eating and being eaten |
| **Plankton** | Small aquatic floating organisms |
| **Food web** | A network of feeding interactions representing interconnected food chains |
| **Trophic level** | Each step in a food chain or food web |
| **Ecological pyramid** | A diagram showing the relative amount of something at each trophic level |
| **Pyramid of energy** | Shows relative energy available at each level (kJ · m⁻² · y⁻¹) |
| **Pyramid of biomass** | Shows relative living organic matter at each level (g · m⁻²); can be inverted |
| **Pyramid of numbers** | Shows the relative number of organisms at each level; can be inverted |

# 3.4 Cycles of Matter

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Recycling in the biosphere

**Unlike the one-way flow of energy, matter is recycled within and between ecosystems.** Elements combine to form the building blocks of organisms.

**Biogeochemical cycles** are the **biological, chemical, and physical processes that transfer elements**. They are **powered by the flow of energy**.

Though not classified as a cycle, **human activity is influential as well** — deforestation, for instance.

## The water cycle

Water **continuously moves between the oceans, the atmosphere, land, and living organisms**.

| Process | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Evaporation** | Liquid water becomes water vapour |
| **Transpiration** | Evaporation from plant leaves |
| **Condensation** | Cooling water vapour condenses into droplets around dust particles |
| **Precipitation** | Water falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail |
| **Runoff** | Flow of water on the surface |
| **Groundwater** | Water absorbed into the soil |
| **Percolation** | Gradual filtering through a porous structure |

**Forms of water:** water vapour, clouds, oceans, rivers and lakes, plants, groundwater, and underground reservoirs.

## Nutrients

A **nutrient** is **a chemical substance that an organism must obtain from its environment to sustain life** — carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus. **Oxygen combines with these elements** and cycles through parts of their journeys.

## The carbon cycle

**Forms of carbon:**

- **Carbon compounds** in living organisms — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids
- **CO₂** in the atmosphere and **dissolved CO₂** in the hydrosphere
- **Carbonate rocks (CaCO₃)**, **fossil fuels** (oil, coal), and **natural gas (CH₄)**

**Processes:** photosynthesis, cellular respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossilisation, combustion, dissolution, deposition.

## The nitrogen cycle

Organisms require nitrogen to make **amino acids**, used to build **proteins and nucleic acids** (which make up DNA and RNA).

**Forms of nitrogen:**

- **Nitrogen gas (N₂)** in the atmosphere
- **Ammonia (NH₃), ammonium (NH₄⁺), nitrate ions (NO₃⁻), and nitrite ions (NO₂⁻)** in soil, waste, and dead or decaying organic matter
- Dissolved nitrogen in several forms in large water bodies

**The processes:**

| Process | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Bacteria in soil and on **legume roots** convert N₂ into NH₃/NH₄⁺. **Lightning** also converts N₂ into usable forms — atmospheric nitrogen fixation |
| **Nitrification** | Soil bacteria convert NH₃/NH₄⁺ into NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻, usable by producers |
| **Assimilation** | Plants absorb NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ from the soil and convert these **inorganic** compounds into **organic** proteins and nucleic acids |
| **Feeding** | Consumers eat producers and assimilate the organic compounds |
| **Decomposition / ammonification** | Decomposers release nitrogen from waste and dead organisms as ammonia, nitrates, and nitrites |
| **Denitrification** | Other soil bacteria convert NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ back to **N₂** in the air |

**Human factors:** **excess fertiliser is carried into surface water or groundwater by precipitation.**

Note that assimilation is the step where nitrogen crosses from **inorganic to organic** — the boundary between the geochemical and the biological halves of the cycle.

## The phosphorus cycle

**Phosphorus forms part of DNA and RNA, but is not abundant in the biosphere.**

**Forms of phosphorus:**

- **Inorganic phosphate (PO₄³⁻)** — rock and soil minerals on land; dissolved or as sediment in the ocean
- **Organic phosphorus compounds** in living things

**Weathering and erosion of rocks gradually release phosphate.** Phosphate then cycles between **soil, producers, and consumers**, while **marine organisms incorporate dissolved phosphate** into compounds.

Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus has **no atmospheric form** — which is why its supply depends on slow rock weathering and why it is so often limiting.

## Nutrient limitation

**The availability of nutrients can limit the primary productivity of an ecosystem** that has ample sunlight and water.

- **Primary productivity** — the rate at which primary producers create organic material such as carbohydrates
- **Limiting nutrient** — the nutrient whose supply limits productivity

**Fertiliser solves the problem of nutrient limitation in soil.**

**Aquatic ecosystems** are often nutrient-poor, with **nitrogen limiting in saltwater** and **phosphorus limiting in freshwater**.

**Large inputs of a limiting nutrient** — runoff from heavily fertilised fields — can produce an **algal bloom**, which can **cover the water's surface and disrupt the ecosystem**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biogeochemical cycle** | Biological, chemical, and physical processes that transfer elements, powered by energy flow |
| **Evaporation** | Liquid water becoming water vapour |
| **Transpiration** | Evaporation from plant leaves |
| **Condensation** | Cooling water vapour condensing into droplets around dust particles |
| **Precipitation** | Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail |
| **Runoff** | Flow of water on the surface |
| **Groundwater** | Water absorbed into the soil |
| **Percolation** | Gradual filtering through a porous structure |
| **Nutrient** | A chemical substance an organism must obtain from its environment to sustain life |
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Bacteria or lightning converting N₂ into NH₃/NH₄⁺ |
| **Nitrification** | Soil bacteria converting NH₃/NH₄⁺ into NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ |
| **Assimilation** | Plants converting inorganic nitrogen compounds into organic proteins and nucleic acids |
| **Ammonification** | Decomposers releasing nitrogen from waste and dead organisms |
| **Denitrification** | Soil bacteria converting NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ back to N₂ |
| **Primary productivity** | The rate at which primary producers create organic material |
| **Limiting nutrient** | The nutrient whose supply limits productivity |
| **Algal bloom** | Rapid algal growth from a large input of a limiting nutrient, disrupting the ecosystem |

# 4.1 Climate

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Weather, climate, and microclimates

- **Weather** — the **day-to-day** condition of Earth's atmosphere
- **Climate** — **year-after-year** patterns of temperature and precipitation
- **Microclimates** are created because **environmental conditions can vary over small distances**

## Factors affecting climate

1. **Solar energy trapped in the biosphere**
2. **Latitude**
3. **The transport of heat by winds and ocean currents**

## The greenhouse effect

1. **Solar energy (sunlight) strikes Earth's surface**
2. Some is **reflected into space**; some is **absorbed and converted into heat (infrared radiation)**
3. Some heat **radiates into space**; some is **trapped by atmospheric gases** — mainly **carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour**

**This phenomenon maintains Earth's average temperature.**

- **More greenhouse gases** → more heat trapped → **Earth warms**
- **Fewer greenhouse gases** → less heat trapped → **Earth cools**

Note the change of form in step 2: sunlight arrives as visible light, which the atmosphere lets through, and leaves as **infrared**, which greenhouse gases absorb. That asymmetry is the whole mechanism.

## Latitude and solar energy

**Solar energy is intense near the equator**, where rays are **concentrated**, while **polar areas receive less intense solar energy**, where rays are **spread out**.

This **unequal distribution creates the tropical, temperate, and polar climate zones**.

## Heat transport in the biosphere

**Warm air** — such as air near the equator — is **less dense and rises**, expanding and spreading north and south, **losing heat along the way**, and **sinking as it cools**.

**Cool air** — such as air near the poles — is **denser and sinks** toward the surface, **pushing surface air outward** and **warming as it travels**, then **rising as it warms**.

**Earth's rotation** makes winds blow **from west to east over temperate zones** and **east to west over the tropics and poles**.

**Ocean currents:** **warm currents add moisture and heat to air**, while **cool currents cool air**. **Deep ocean currents are caused by cold water near the poles sinking**, and that water **rises in warmer regions through upwelling**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Weather** | The day-to-day condition of Earth's atmosphere |
| **Climate** | Year-after-year patterns of temperature and precipitation |
| **Microclimate** | Local variation in environmental conditions over small distances |
| **Greenhouse effect** | Atmospheric gases trapping heat radiated from Earth's surface, maintaining average temperature |
| **Greenhouse gases** | Mainly carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour |
| **Climate zones** | Tropical, temperate, and polar, created by unequal solar distribution |
| **Upwelling** | The rising of deep cold water in warmer regions |

# 4.2 Niches and Community Interactions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The niche

**Tolerance** is the **ability to survive and reproduce under a range of environmental conditions**. Outside their **optimum range of tolerance**, organisms **experience stress**, expending **more energy on homeostasis and less on growth and reproduction**.

**Habitat** is **the place where an organism lives**, determined by its **range of tolerance**.

**Niche** is **the role or position an organism has in its environment**, and is **unique to each species**. It comprises habitat, activity patterns, the resources it obtains, and more:

- **Physical aspects** — abiotic factors such as water or temperature
- **Biological aspects** — biotic factors such as reproduction and diet

A **resource** is a **necessity of life** — water, nutrients, light, food, space.

The distinction to keep: a **habitat is where an organism lives**, a **niche is what it does there**.

## Competition

**Competition** occurs when organisms **attempt to use the same limited ecological resource in the same place at the same time**. It is **intraspecific** (within the same species) or **interspecific** (between different species).

Competition **shapes an ecosystem** by:

- Determining the **number and kinds of species**
- Determining the **niche each species occupies**
- Causing species to **divide resources**

## The competitive exclusion principle

**No two species can occupy exactly the same niche in exactly the same habitat at exactly the same time** — one will outcompete the other for resources.

**As a result, species usually divide resources.**

## Predation, herbivory, and keystone species

**Predation** — an interaction in which **one animal (the predator) captures and feeds on another animal (the prey)**. It can affect the **size of prey populations and where prey can live and feed**.

**Herbivory** — an interaction in which **one animal (the herbivore) feeds on producers** such as plants. It can affect the **size and distribution of plant populations** and **where plants can survive and grow**.

**Keystone species** — **a non-producer species that has a disproportionately large effect on its community relative to its abundance**, where changes in its population **cause dramatic changes in the structure of a community**.

Examples: **sea otters** (sea-urchin eaters) and **beavers and elephants** (habitat creators).

The definition is precise in a way worth noting: the effect must be **large relative to abundance**. A numerous species with a large effect is not a keystone species.

## Symbioses

**Symbioses** are relationships in which **two species live closely together**.

| Type | Effect | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mutualism** | **+/+** | Both benefit | Clownfish and anemone; rhinoceros and tickbird |
| **Parasitism** | **+/−** | One organism lives in or on another and **harms** it. Generally parasites **weaken but do not kill** their host | Tapeworms (in host); fleas, ticks, lice, leeches, mosquitoes (on host) |
| **Commensalism** | **+/0** | One benefits, the other is neither helped nor harmed | Barnacles and grey whales; remoras and sharks |

That parasites usually **weaken rather than kill** is not incidental — a parasite that kills its host quickly loses its own habitat.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Tolerance** | The ability to survive and reproduce under a range of environmental conditions |
| **Habitat** | The place where an organism lives, determined by its range of tolerance |
| **Niche** | The role or position an organism has in its environment, unique to each species |
| **Resource** | A necessity of life — water, nutrients, light, food, space |
| **Competition** | Organisms using the same limited resource in the same place at the same time |
| **Intraspecific competition** | Competition within the same species |
| **Interspecific competition** | Competition between different species |
| **Competitive exclusion principle** | No two species can occupy exactly the same niche in the same habitat at the same time |
| **Predation** | One animal captures and feeds on another |
| **Herbivory** | One animal feeds on producers |
| **Keystone species** | A non-producer with a disproportionately large effect relative to its abundance |
| **Symbiosis** | A relationship in which two species live closely together |
| **Mutualism** | A symbiosis where both benefit (+/+) |
| **Parasitism** | A symbiosis where one lives in or on another and harms it (+/−) |
| **Commensalism** | A symbiosis where one benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0) |

# 4.3 Succession

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ecological succession

**Ecological succession** is **a series of more-or-less predictable changes that occur in a community over time**.

## Primary succession

**Primary succession** is **the establishment of a community in an area of exposed rock that does not have any topsoil**. **Early stages can be very slow.**

**Pioneer species** are **the first species to colonise barren areas**. The sequence:

1. **Lichen** — a **mutualistic symbiosis between a fungus and an alga** — **fixes atmospheric N₂, breaks down rock, and adds organic material to form soil**
2. **Mosses**, which are simple plants
3. **Ferns, herbs, and small shrubs** arrive and change the environment further
4. **Trees** arrive, and their leaves **provide shade and a cooler temperature**
5. Over time, **more and more species find a suitable niche and survive**

Each stage makes the next possible by changing conditions — which is why succession is predictable rather than random.

**Primary succession often follows:**

- **Volcanic explosions** creating new land or sterilising existing areas
- **Retreating glaciers** leaving only exposed bare rock

## Secondary succession

**Secondary succession** occurs **where existing communities are not completely destroyed by disturbances**. It **proceeds faster than primary succession** because **seeds, roots, and soil are present**.

**It often follows:**

- **Wildfires**, which destroy many plants but **stimulate seed growth**
- **Hurricanes** or other natural disturbances
- **Human activities** such as logging and farming

## Climax communities

**Climax communities** are **ecological communities in the final stage of succession, in which the species composition is relatively stable**.

**Natural disturbances are common in many communities**, and **secondary succession in healthy ecosystems following them often reproduces the original climax community**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ecological succession** | A series of more-or-less predictable changes occurring in a community over time |
| **Primary succession** | The establishment of a community on exposed rock with no topsoil |
| **Pioneer species** | The first species to colonise barren areas |
| **Lichen** | A mutualistic symbiosis between a fungus and an alga; a pioneer species |
| **Secondary succession** | Succession where existing communities were not completely destroyed; faster, as soil remains |
| **Climax community** | An ecological community in the final stage of succession, relatively stable in composition |

# 4.4 Biomes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What shapes a biome

**Regional climates can be affected by proximity to oceans or mountain ranges** — cold and warm ocean currents, and the leeward or windward side of a mountain.

**Biomes are described in terms of abiotic factors** like climate and soil type, **and biotic factors** like plant and animal life.

## The ten major biomes

### 1. Tropical rainforest

Tall trees form a dense covering called a **canopy**, 50–80 m above the forest floor. Below, shorter trees and vines form a layer called the **understory**.

- **Abiotic:** high precipitation; **nutrient-poor soil**
- **Plant life:** large leaves maximise sunlight in the understory; tall trees have **buttress roots**; **epiphytic** plants grow on the branches of tall trees (**commensalism**)
- **Animal life:** camouflage, colour-changing, climbing, jumping, and flight adaptations

### 2. Tropical dry forest

Rainy and dry seasons, with droughts following periods of rain.

- **Abiotic:** warm year-round; **rich soil**
- **Plant life:** **deciduous**, waxy leaves; store water in tissues to survive dry seasons
- **Animal life:** enter **estivation** (roughly, hibernation) or migrate during dry seasons

### 3. Tropical grassland / savanna / shrubland

Medium-to-low rainfall, spotted with isolated trees and small groves.

- **Abiotic:** warm; seasonal rain; compact soils; **frequent fires**
- **Plant life:** deciduous, waxy-leaved plants; grass unappetising due to **high silica**
- **Animal life:** migrate, or burrow and remain dormant in dry seasons

### 4. Desert

- **Abiotic:** low precipitation; varying temperature; mineral-rich but organic-material-poor soil
- **Plant life:** store water in tissues, minimise leaf surface area, **only open pores at night**
- **Animal life:** often **nocturnal**; large ears and other extremities to lose body heat

### 5. Temperate grassland

- **Abiotic:** seasonal temperature change; moderate rain; **fertile soil**; occasional fires
- **Plant life:** resistant to grazing and fire; seed dispersal by wind
- **Animal life:** constant threat of predation, met with camouflage and burrowing

### 6. Temperate woodland and shrubland

Large areas of grass and wildflowers interspersed with trees.

- **Abiotic:** hot dry summers; cool moist winters; thin, nutrient-poor soils; periodic fires
- **Plant life:** waxy leaves, fire resistant
- **Animal life:** **browsers** with varied diets of vegetation; camouflage is common

### 7. Temperate forest

Fertile soils rich in **humus**, a material formed from decaying leaves and other organic matter.

- **Abiotic:** cold to moderate winters; warm summers; year-round precipitation; fertile soil
- **Plant life:** **deciduous** trees go dormant in winter; **conifers** have needle-shaped, wax-coated leaves to minimise water loss
- **Animal life:** many hibernate or migrate; others have winter camouflage

### 8. Northwestern coniferous forest

- **Abiotic:** mild temperature; cool dry summers; abundant rain outside summer; rocky acidic soil
- **Plant life:** low diversity; lush, dense growth; tall trees
- **Animal life:** camouflage; browsers

### 9. Boreal forest (taiga)

- **Abiotic:** long cold winters; short mild summers; moderate precipitation; high humidity; acidic, nutrient-poor soils
- **Plant life:** conifers' **conical shape sheds snow**, **dark colour absorbs heat**, waxy leaves
- **Animal life:** extra insulation in fat or downy feathers, or migration for winter

### 10. Tundra

**Permafrost**, a layer of permanently frozen subsoil, **limits plant height**.

- **Abiotic:** strong winds; low precipitation; short soggy summers; long, cold, dark winters; poorly developed soils; permafrost
- **Plant life:** mosses and other plants **grow low to avoid strong winds**; legumes have **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** to cope with poor soil; wind seed dispersal is common
- **Animal life:** many migrate to avoid winter; year-round residents have **natural antifreeze**, **small extremities** limiting heat loss, and a varied diet

Across all ten, the adaptations are answers to whichever abiotic factor is most limiting — water in the desert, cold in the tundra, light in the rainforest understory.

## Other land areas

**Mountain ranges and polar ice caps are not easily defined in terms of a typical community** of plants and animals, and are **not usually classified into biomes**.

- **Mountain ranges** exist on all continents and in many biomes; conditions — temperature, wind, soil, organisms — **vary greatly by altitude**
- **Polar ice caps** border the tundra and are **cold year-round**, with few plants, though **algae sometimes grow on snow and ice** and mosses and lichens appear seasonally. Animals include marine mammals

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biome** | A region described by abiotic factors such as climate and soil and biotic factors such as plant and animal life |
| **Canopy** | The dense covering formed by tall trees, 50–80 m above the rainforest floor |
| **Understory** | The layer of shorter trees and vines below the canopy |
| **Epiphyte** | A plant growing on the branches of tall trees, in commensalism |
| **Deciduous** | Shedding leaves seasonally |
| **Estivation** | A dormant state entered during dry seasons, roughly equivalent to hibernation |
| **Browser** | An animal with a varied diet of vegetation |
| **Humus** | Material formed from decaying leaves and other organic matter, making soil fertile |
| **Coniferous** | Bearing needle-shaped, wax-coated leaves that minimise water loss |
| **Taiga** | The boreal forest biome |
| **Permafrost** | A layer of permanently frozen subsoil that limits plant height |

# 4.5 Aquatic Ecosystems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Water depth

| Zone | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Photic zone** | The **sunlit region near the surface** where **photosynthesis takes place**. May be as deep as **200 metres in seas** or **a few metres in rivers** |
| **Aphotic zone** | **Below the photic zone**; no photosynthesis, so **chemosynthesis** instead |
| **Benthic zone** | The **bottoms of water bodies** |

- **Phytoplankton** — unicellular
- **Zooplankton** — planktonic animals
- **Benthos** — organisms **attached to or resting on the bottom**, mostly **filter feeders**

Note the range on the photic zone: it is defined by **light penetration, not by depth**, which is why it is 200 m in clear ocean and a few metres in a silty river.

## Freshwater ecosystems

**Rivers and streams** — **high oxygen level**, running water. Water flows from **head** — underground springs or snowmelt — to **mouth**, where the flowing water empties out.

**Lakes and ponds** — an inland body of **standing water**.

**Wetland** — a place where **water covers soil or is present at or near the surface for at least part of the year**. Wetlands are **good for agriculture** and are **breeding grounds for many organisms**. They **purify water by filtering pollutants** and **help prevent flooding by absorbing and slowly releasing large amounts of water**.

Three types, distinguished by vegetation:

- **Bogs** — decaying peat moss
- **Marshes** — a variety of reeds and grasses
- **Swamps** — woody plants and trees

## Estuaries

**Estuaries** are **saltwater wetlands** where a **freshwater river meets the salty sea**, containing a **mixture of fresh and salt water**. They are **spawning and nursery grounds** for many ecologically and commercially important fish and shellfish species.

- **Salt marsh** — temperate estuaries
- **Mangrove swamp** — tropical estuaries, **tolerant of high salt concentration**

## The ocean

**Intertidal zone** — a **narrow band where ocean meets land**. Communities are **constantly changing** because of disturbances such as **daily tides**. Organisms are **submerged in sea water at high tide and exposed to air and sunlight at low tide**. **Barnacles** — small saltwater animals with a shell-like cover — **and seaweed permanently attach themselves to the rocks**.

**Coastal ocean** — extends from the **low-tide mark to the outer edge of the continental shelf**, the **relatively shallow border surrounding the continent**. **Kelp forests and coral reefs** are important coastal communities.

**Open ocean** — begins at the edge of the continental shelf and extends outward, covering **more than 90% of the world's ocean**.

- **Photic zone** — **low nutrient level**, supporting only the smallest species of phytoplankton
- **Aphotic zone** — **permanently dark**, containing **deep-sea vents** in the deepest parts of the ocean

## Keywords

| **Photic zone** | The sunlit surface region where photosynthesis takes place |
| **Aphotic zone** | The region below the photic zone, where chemosynthesis replaces photosynthesis |
| **Benthic zone** | The bottoms of water bodies |
| **Phytoplankton** | Unicellular photosynthetic plankton |
| **Zooplankton** | Planktonic animals |
| **Benthos** | Organisms attached to or resting on the bottom, mostly filter feeders |
| **Head** | The source of a river — underground springs or snowmelt |
| **Mouth** | Where flowing water empties out |
| **Wetland** | A place where water covers soil or is near the surface for at least part of the year |
| **Bog** | A wetland of decaying peat moss |
| **Marsh** | A wetland of reeds and grasses |
| **Swamp** | A wetland of woody plants and trees |
| **Estuary** | A saltwater wetland where a freshwater river meets the sea |
| **Intertidal zone** | The narrow band where ocean meets land, submerged at high tide and exposed at low tide |
| **Continental shelf** | The relatively shallow border surrounding a continent |

# 5.1 How Populations Grow

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Describing populations

Researchers study **geographic range, density and distribution, growth rate, and age structure**.

**Geographic range** — the **area inhabited by a population**, depending on species; large or small, and in a specific location.

## Density and distribution

**Population density** — **the number of individuals per unit area**. No unit conversion is involved: 4,000 goats in 80 km² is simply **50 goats per km²**.

### Estimating population size

**Random quadrat sampling** — count the number in **small, randomly located squares** within the total area, then project the result onto the total area. Coverage for plants uses quadrats.

$$\text{Population size} = \frac{\text{mean number per quadrat} \times \text{total area}}{\text{area of each quadrat}}$$

**Capture–mark–release (the Lincoln Index):**

$$\text{Population size} = \frac{n_1 \times n_2}{n_3}$$

where $n_1$ is the number initially caught and marked, $n_2$ the number caught the second time, and $n_3$ the number of marked individuals in the second sample.

**This could be inaccurate** — because of **emigration and immigration**, among other factors.

### Spatial distribution

**Spatial distribution** is **the pattern of spacing of a population**:

| Pattern | Description | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **Clumped / clustered** | Aggregated in patches | Resource availability and behaviour |
| **Uniform** | Evenly spaced | Social interactions, such as territory |
| **Random** | Independent position | No strong attractions or repulsions |

## Growth rate

**Growth rate** determines whether a population **increases, decreases, or stays the same**:

| Growth | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Zero** | Birth rate **=** death rate |
| **Positive** | Birth rate **>** death rate |
| **Negative** | Birth rate **<** death rate |

$$\text{growth rate} = \frac{P_{\text{final}} - P_{\text{initial}}}{P_{\text{initial}}}$$

## Factors affecting population size

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Natality** | Number of births, per 1,000 people per year |
| **Mortality** | Number of deaths, per 1,000 people per year |
| **Immigration** | Members arriving |
| **Emigration** | Members leaving |

## Age structure

**Age structure** is **the number of males and females of each age a population contains**.

## Population growth

**Exponential growth** produces a **J curve**, with a **constant growth rate**. It begins with a **lag phase** of slow growth.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Geographic range** | The area inhabited by a population |
| **Population density** | The number of individuals per unit area |
| **Random quadrat sampling** | Counting organisms in small randomly located squares and projecting onto the total area |
| **Lincoln Index** | The capture–mark–release estimate, (n₁ × n₂) / n₃ |
| **Spatial distribution** | The pattern of spacing of a population — clumped, uniform, or random |
| **Growth rate** | Whether a population increases, decreases, or stays the same |
| **Natality** | Number of births per 1,000 per year |
| **Mortality** | Number of deaths per 1,000 per year |
| **Immigration** | Members arriving |
| **Emigration** | Members leaving |
| **Age structure** | The number of males and females of each age in a population |
| **Exponential growth** | Growth at a constant rate, producing a J curve |
| **Lag phase** | The slow-growth period at the start of exponential growth |

## Logistic growth

**Logistic growth** produces an **S curve**. It occurs when a population's growth **slows or stops following exponential growth, at the population's carrying capacity**.

**All populations grow exponentially until a limiting factor slows the growth.**

**Carrying capacity** is the **maximum number of individuals of a species that an environment can support long term**. It is limited by **energy, resources, predation, disease, and disturbances**.

**Oscillation** occurs when a species reaches the carrying capacity and there is an **overshoot**, causing **fierce competition**; other limiting factors then push the population to **die back**, and the process repeats.

**Phases of growth:**

- **Exponential growth** — unlimited resources, so individuals reproduce and grow rapidly
- **Transitional phase** — the **rate** of population growth slows, but the population **size does not decrease**

The transitional phase is the one most often misread: growth slowing is not the same as the population shrinking.

# 5.2 Limits to Growth

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Population size is limited by **competition, predation, parasitism, unusual weather, and natural disaster**.

**Limiting factors:**

- **Control the growth** of a population
- **Determine the carrying capacity** of an environment for a species

They divide into **density-dependent** and **density-independent**.

## Density-dependent factors

A density-dependent factor **operates strongly only when the population reaches a certain level**.

**Competition** — organisms compete for resources, which **lowers the birth rate and increases the death rate**. It may be **interspecific or intraspecific**, and **can lead to resource division**.

**Predation and herbivory** — populations of both groups **cycle up and down over time**. This can produce **predator-mediated competition**.

**Parasitism and disease** — **the denser the host population, the more easily parasites or pathogens spread** from one host to another, and **the death rate increases**.

**Stress from overcrowding** — high levels of stress cause **weakened immunity**; **females neglect, kill, or eat their own offspring**; the **birth rate declines and the death rate increases**; and there are **increased rates of emigration**.

What unites them is the dependence on **density**: each becomes more severe as individuals are packed closer together, which is what allows them to hold a population near its carrying capacity.

## Density-independent factors

Density-independent factors **affect all populations in similar ways** — **environmental changes regardless of population size, age, and density**.

## Top-down and bottom-up factors

Limiting factors may act from the **top down** (predators controlling prey) or the **bottom up** (resource supply controlling producers).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Limiting factor** | A factor controlling population growth and determining carrying capacity |
| **Density-dependent factor** | A factor operating strongly only once a population reaches a certain level |
| **Density-independent factor** | A factor affecting all populations similarly, regardless of size, age, or density |
| **Predator-mediated competition** | Competition among prey shaped by the action of a predator |

# 5.3 Human Population Growth

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Demography** is **the study of human population**.

## Thomas Malthus

Malthus argued that **war, famine, and disease will slow down population growth**.

## The demographic transition

Five stages:

| Stage | Birth rate | Death rate | Conditions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **High** | **High** | Harsh environment — poor sanitation and nutrition |
| **2** | **High** | **Falls rapidly** | Better conditions |
| **3** | **Falling** | Falls slowly | — |
| **4** | **Low** | **Low** | — |
| **5** | High **or** low — debated | Low | — |

Stage 2 is where population grows fastest, and the reason is the **gap** between the two rates: the death rate falls quickly while the birth rate is still high, and growth is the difference between them.

**Stage 5 is unsettled** — whether the birth rate ends up high or low is a matter of debate, while the death rate stays low.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Demography** | The study of human population |
| **Demographic transition** | The five-stage model of changing birth and death rates as conditions improve |

# 6.1 A Changing Landscape

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Effects of human activity

Humans affect regional and global environments through **agriculture, development, and industry**. These impact the quality of **Earth's natural resources — soil, water, and the atmosphere**.

### Agriculture

**Monoculture** is **clearing large areas to plant one highly productive crop every year**, such as soybeans.

- It **enables efficient sorting, tending, and harvesting of crops using machines**
- It **impacts freshwater and fertile soil**
- **Fertiliser production and farm machinery consume large amounts of fossil fuels**

Note that monoculture is not simply a mistake — the efficiency is real, and it is what makes the practice hard to give up.

### Development

**Dense human communities produce large amounts of waste.** If not disposed of, waste **affects air, water, and soil resources**. Development also **consumes farmland and fragments natural habitats**.

### Industrial growth

**Modern conveniences require large amounts of energy to produce and power.** **Burning fossil fuels** — coal, oil, natural gas — **affects the environment**, and **manufacturing and energy production waste is often discarded directly into the air, water, and soil**.

## Ecosystem goods and services

**The goods and services produced by healthy ecosystems benefit the human economy.** **Society must pay if the environment cannot provide them** — breathable air and drinkable water being the examples.

## Resources

| Type | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Renewable resource** | Can be **produced or replaced by a healthy ecosystem** | Wind, solar energy, water, trees |
| **Nonrenewable resource** | **Cannot be replenished within a reasonable amount of time** | Coal, oil, natural gas |

## Sustainable development

**Sustainable development** means **providing for human needs while protecting the ecosystems that produce natural resources** — **using resources at a replaceable rate while preserving the biosphere's environmental health**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Monoculture** | Clearing large areas to plant one highly productive crop every year |
| **Ecosystem goods and services** | The goods and services produced by healthy ecosystems that benefit the human economy |
| **Renewable resource** | A resource that can be produced or replaced by a healthy ecosystem |
| **Nonrenewable resource** | A resource that cannot be replenished within a reasonable amount of time |
| **Sustainable development** | Providing for human needs while protecting the ecosystems that produce natural resources |

# 6.2 Using Resources Wisely

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Soil resources

**Healthy soil supports both agriculture and forestry.**

**Topsoil** is **the mineral- and nutrient-rich portion of soil**.

| Threat | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Soil erosion** | The **removal of soil by water or wind** |
| **Desertification** | A combination of **farming, overgrazing, seasonal drought, and climate change** that **turns farmland into desert** |
| **Deforestation** | **Loss of forests**, which may lead to **severe erosion**, especially when followed by grazing and ploughing |

### Soil use and sustainability

- Leaving **stems and roots of previous crops** to hold soil in place between plantings
- **Crop rotation** — varying crops seasonally or yearly to **prevent erosion and nutrient loss**
- **Contour ploughing** — planting fields of crops **across, instead of down, the slope** of the land
- **Terracing** — shaping the land to create level **"steps"**
- **Forestry** — **selectively harvesting mature trees** to promote the growth of younger trees

The first three all attack the same problem: water running downhill carries soil with it, so anything that slows or interrupts that flow preserves the topsoil.

## Freshwater resources

Humans depend on fresh water and freshwater ecosystems for **drinking water, industry, transportation, energy, and waste disposal**.

A **pollutant** is **a harmful material that can enter the biosphere**.

- **Single point sources** — pollutants from a **single source**, such as a factory or an oil spill
- **Nonpoint sources** — pollutants from **many smaller sources**, such as grease washed off streets

### Primary sources of water pollution

**Nonpoint sources.**

**Industrial and agricultural chemicals**, which lead to **biological magnification**.

**Biological magnification** is **the process through which small amounts of pollutants picked up by primary producers increase to dangerous amounts at high trophic levels**, if not eliminated or broken down.

- **PCBs** — organic chemicals widely used in industry
- **DDT** — a pesticide used in agriculture

**Residential sewage**, which is **rich in nitrogen and phosphorus** and can **stimulate blooms of bacteria and algae** that **rob water of oxygen**, leaving oxygen-poor **"dead zones"**.

Biological magnification is why a concentration harmless to plankton can be lethal to a top predator: each trophic level concentrates what the level below it accumulated.

### Water quality and sustainability

A **watershed** **includes all land whose groundwater, streams, and rivers drain into the same place**, such as a large lake or river.

**Densely growing plants in wetlands, forests, and other vegetation absorb excess nutrients and filter out certain pollutants, purifying water.**

## Atmospheric resources

**Smog** is **a grey-brown haze formed by chemical reactions among pollutants**, released into the air by **industrial processes and automobile exhaust**. One product is **ozone**, which **threatens people's health at ground level**.

**Acid rain** results from pollutants reacting in the atmosphere.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Topsoil** | The mineral- and nutrient-rich portion of soil |
| **Soil erosion** | The removal of soil by water or wind |
| **Desertification** | Farming, overgrazing, drought, and climate change turning farmland into desert |
| **Deforestation** | Loss of forests, which may lead to severe erosion |
| **Crop rotation** | Varying crops seasonally or yearly to prevent erosion and nutrient loss |
| **Contour ploughing** | Planting across, rather than down, the slope of the land |
| **Terracing** | Shaping land into level steps |
| **Pollutant** | A harmful material that can enter the biosphere |
| **Single point source** | A pollutant from one source, such as a factory or oil spill |
| **Nonpoint source** | Pollutants from many smaller sources |
| **Biological magnification** | Small amounts of pollutant in producers increasing to dangerous amounts at high trophic levels |
| **Dead zone** | An oxygen-poor area created when blooms rob water of oxygen |
| **Watershed** | All land whose groundwater, streams, and rivers drain into the same place |
| **Smog** | A grey-brown haze formed by chemical reactions among pollutants |
| **Acid rain** | Rain made acidic by pollutants reacting in the atmosphere |

## Air pollution in detail

**Acid rain** — **nitrogen and sulfur compounds released by burning fossil fuels can form nitric and sulfuric acids in the air**. It:

- **Kills plants by damaging leaves**
- **Changes the chemistry of soil and surface water**
- **Dissolves and releases mercury and other toxic elements from soils**

**Greenhouse gases** — **burning fossil fuels and forests releases stored carbon as carbon dioxide**, and **agricultural practices such as raising cattle and farming rice release methane**. **Excess accumulation of greenhouse gases leads to global warming and climate change.**

**Particulates** — **microscopic particles of ash and dust**, released by certain industrial processes and some kinds of diesel engines. They **can cause serious health problems if they enter the lungs**.

## Air quality and sustainability

**Automobile emission standards and clean-air regulations** have had measurable effects: in **1996 the sale of leaded gasoline was banned in the US**, and **lead levels in soils, rivers, and streams around the country have dropped**.

# 6.3 Biodiversity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The basics of biodiversity

**Biological diversity (biodiversity)** is **the total of all the genetically based variation in all organisms in the biosphere**.

It has three levels:

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ecosystem diversity** | The variety of **habitats, communities, and ecological processes** |
| **Species diversity** | The **number of different species** in the biosphere or a certain area |
| **Genetic diversity** | The total of **all different forms of genes present in a species** |

## Measuring diversity

Two components:

- **Richness** — **the number of different species present**
- **Evenness** — **how similar the abundance of each species present is**

**Simpson's Diversity Index** **considers both richness and evenness**, where $n$ is the total number of organisms of a particular species and $N$ the total number of organisms of all species.

**A higher D value means greater biodiversity.** The **maximum D = 1** (infinite diversity) and the **minimum D = 0** (no diversity).

Both components are needed: a community with many species but one overwhelmingly dominant is less diverse than one with the same species in similar abundance, and richness alone cannot see the difference.

## Valuing biodiversity

**Medical value** — **wild species are the original source of many medicines**, such as painkillers like **aspirin** and antibiotics like **penicillin**.

**Agricultural value** — **wild plants may carry genes we can use**, such as **disease resistance or pest resistance**.

**Ecosystem value** — **the number and variety of species in an ecosystem can influence that ecosystem's stability, productivity, and value to humans**.

## Threats to biodiversity

**Altered habitats.** **Habitat fragmentation** is **development or agriculture splitting ecosystems into pieces**.

**Climate change.** If conditions change **beyond an organism's tolerance**, it must **migrate or go extinct**. **Species in fragmented habitats are more vulnerable, as they may be unable to migrate.**

That last sentence connects the two threats: fragmentation is dangerous partly on its own, and much more dangerous once the climate starts moving, because it removes the escape route.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biodiversity** | The total of all genetically based variation in all organisms in the biosphere |
| **Ecosystem diversity** | The variety of habitats, communities, and ecological processes |
| **Species diversity** | The number of different species in the biosphere or an area |
| **Genetic diversity** | The total of all different forms of genes present in a species |
| **Richness** | The number of different species present |
| **Evenness** | How similar the abundance of each species present is |
| **Simpson's Diversity Index** | A measure considering both richness and evenness; D = 1 is maximum, D = 0 minimum |
| **Habitat fragmentation** | Development or agriculture splitting ecosystems into pieces |
| **Ecological hot spot** | An area of exceptional biodiversity under threat |

# 16.1 Darwin's Voyage of Discovery

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Charles Darwin** (born **12 February 1809**) **published convincing evidence that species evolve, with a reasonable explanation**.

## Patterns of biological diversity

**Vary globally** — species inhabited **separated but ecologically similar habitats** around the globe. They are **similar not because they are closely related, only because of similar environments** — emus, rheas, and ostriches.

**Vary locally** — species occupied **different habitats within a local area**. In the Galápagos Islands, different types of **birds and turtles**.

**Vary over time** — **fossils of extinct animals are similar to living species**.

**Fossils** are **preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms**.

The three patterns each isolate a different variable — space at global scale, space at local scale, and time — and each shows the same thing: species are not fixed.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Fossil** | Preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms |

# 16.2 Ideas That Shaped Darwin's Thinking

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## James Hutton

**1785: Theory of Geological Change.**

## Charles Lyell

***Principles of Geology*** proposed that **current geological processes are the same as those which shaped Earth millions of years ago** — and **Darwin found evidence to prove this**.

## Jean-Baptiste Lamarck

**1809: Hypothesis of the Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics.**

**Acquired characteristics** are **traits altered by an individual organism during its life**. Lamarck proposed that:

- **Use or disuse of a body part could cause change in features within the lifetime** of that organism
- Those **changes would be passed on to offspring**

The standard example is **giraffes having long necks**.

**Evaluation — the hypothesis is incorrect:**

- **Evolution occurs in populations, not individuals**
- **Evolution does not mean species are becoming better; there is no direction for evolution**

**However, Lamarck was among the first to suggest species changed** and to **explain evolution scientifically using natural processes.** That is why he appears here at all: the mechanism was wrong, the question was right.

## Thomas Malthus

**1798: Principle of Populations**, stating that **if the human population grew unchecked, there would not be enough food and living space for everyone**.

## Artificial selection

**Nature provides variations, and humans select useful ones** — which **requires inherited variation**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Acquired characteristics** | Traits altered by an individual organism during its life through use or disuse |
| **Principle of Populations** | Malthus's argument that unchecked population growth outruns food and living space |
| **Artificial selection** | Humans selecting useful variations that nature provides, requiring inherited variation |

# 16.3 Darwin Presents His Case

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**1858 — *On the Origin of Species*** outlined the ideas of **evolution by natural selection**, resting on **three principles**.

## 1. Struggle for existence

**If more individuals are produced than can survive, the population competes to obtain food, living space, and other limited necessities of life.**

For example, **only 50% of bears survive past one year**.

## 2. Variation and adaptation

**Individuals in a population vary in heritable characteristics.**

An **adaptation** is a **heritable characteristic that increases an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment** — camouflage, mimicry, and behaviours.

## 3. Survival of the fittest

**Fitness** is **how well an organism can survive and reproduce in its environment**.

**Survival of the fittest** is **the difference in rates of survival and reproduction** that **passes hereditary adaptations to the next generation**.

## Natural selection

**Natural selection** is **the process by which organisms with variations most suited to the local environment survive and leave more offspring**.

Its properties:

- **Fitness is influenced by the environment**
- **Well-adapted individuals survive and reproduce**
- **Populations change as the environment changes**
- It **acts on inherited traits**
- It **does not make organisms "better" or move in a fixed direction** — the peppered moth being the example

The third and fifth points belong together: because the environment changes, what counts as well-adapted changes too, which is why there is no fixed direction.

## Descent with modification

Darwin proposed that **over generations, adaptation could cause successful species to evolve into new species**.

**Descent with modification** means **living species are descended, with modification, from common ancestors** — supported by the **fossil record**, and observable in **antibiotic resistance in bacteria**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Struggle for existence** | Competition for limited necessities when more individuals are produced than can survive |
| **Adaptation** | A heritable characteristic increasing an organism's ability to survive and reproduce |
| **Fitness** | How well an organism can survive and reproduce in its environment |
| **Survival of the fittest** | The difference in rates of survival and reproduction that passes adaptations on |
| **Natural selection** | The process by which organisms best suited to the local environment survive and leave more offspring |
| **Descent with modification** | Living species being descended, with modification, from common ancestors |

# 16.4 Evidence of Evolution

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Biogeography

**Biogeography** is **the study of where organisms live now and where they and their ancestors lived in the past**. It reveals two contrasting patterns.

**Pattern 1: Adaptive radiation.** **One species evolved into several different forms adapted to different environments**, and these **new forms share a common ancestor**. The Galápagos Islands had **13 finch species adapted to different diets**, evolved from the **single type seen on the mainland**.

**Pattern 2: Convergent evolution.** **Unrelated organisms live in and adapt to similar environments and come to resemble one another**, with **no recent common ancestor**. **Dolphins, penguins, and fish each independently evolved the ability to swim.**

The two patterns are opposites: **one ancestor producing many forms**, versus **many ancestors producing one form**.

## The age of Earth and fossils

**The Earth is 4.5 billion years old.**

**Fossils** are **preserved remains or imprints of an organism that lived long ago**. **Intermediate fossil forms show the evolution of modern species from extinct ancestors** — **whales evolved from land-dwelling mammals**.

## Comparing anatomy and embryology

| Structure | Definition | Evidence of common ancestor? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Homologous structures** | Structures **adapted for different functions but sharing many similarities** | **Yes** | Forelimbs (five digits) in tetrapods — amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals |
| **Vestigial structures** | Structures **inherited from ancestors that have lost much of their original function** due to different selection pressures | **Yes** | Hind limbs of whales and dolphins |
| **Analogous structures** | Body parts sharing **a common function but not a common structure** | **NOT evidence** | Bee wings and bird wings |

**Comparative embryology** — **similar patterns of embryo development** are evidence of a common ancestor. **All vertebrate embryos exhibit common structures.**

The rule underlying the table: **shared structure implies shared ancestry; shared function does not.** Analogous structures are convergent evolution seen anatomically.

## Genetics and molecular biology

**All living organisms use the same universal genetic code.** **Similarities in DNA, RNA, and protein sequences are evidence of a common ancestor.**

- **Homologous genes** — **Hox genes** determine the **head-to-tail axis**, and are found in **almost all multicellular animals**
- **Homologous proteins** — **cytochrome c** functions in **cellular respiration**, and versions are found in **almost all living cells**

## Testing natural selection

**The Grants documented that natural selection happens in wild finch populations frequently.**

**Variation in a species increases the chance of it surviving environmental change.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biogeography** | The study of where organisms live now and where they and their ancestors lived |
| **Adaptive radiation** | One species evolving into several forms adapted to different environments, sharing a common ancestor |
| **Convergent evolution** | Unrelated organisms in similar environments coming to resemble one another |
| **Fossil** | Preserved remains or imprints of an organism that lived long ago |
| **Homologous structures** | Structures adapted for different functions but sharing similarities; evidence of common ancestry |
| **Vestigial structures** | Structures inherited from ancestors that have lost much of their original function |
| **Analogous structures** | Body parts sharing a function but not a structure; not evidence of common ancestry |
| **Comparative embryology** | Similar patterns of embryo development, evidence of a common ancestor |
| **Homologous genes** | Corresponding genes across species, such as Hox genes |
| **Homologous proteins** | Corresponding proteins across species, such as cytochrome c |

## The vocabulary of heredity

**Genetics** is **the scientific study of heredity**.

| **Gene** | The **basic unit of heredity** that determines traits — a **specific fragment of DNA on a chromosome** |

## Populations and gene pools

A **gene pool** is **all the genes — including all the different alleles for each gene — present in a population**.

**Allele frequency** is **how often a particular allele occurs in a gene pool, compared to other alleles for the same gene**.

## Chromosomes, genotype, and phenotype

**Homologous chromosomes** are a **pair of chromosomes of the same length and shape**, carrying the **same genes in the same order at the same positions**.

**Genotype** is the **particular combination of alleles an organism carries**. It determines a trait **together with environmental conditions**.

- **Homozygous** — the **same** alleles, e.g. **PP** or **pp**
- **Heterozygous** — **different** alleles, e.g. **Pp**

**Phenotype** is **all the physical, physiological, and behavioural characteristics** of an organism.

Note that genotype alone does not fix the phenotype — the environment contributes, which is why identical genotypes can produce different organisms.

# 17.2 Evolution as Genetic Change in Populations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Natural selection on single-gene and polygenic traits

Both follow the same chain:

- **Single-gene traits:** selection on a **particular phenotype** → change in allele frequency → **evolution**
- **Polygenic traits:** selection on a **range of phenotypes** → change in allele frequency → **evolution**

Selection on polygenic traits takes **three forms**.

## Three types of selection

**Directional selection** — **selection on one extreme end of phenotypes**, occurring **when individuals at one end of the curve have higher fitness** than those in the middle or at the other end.
*Example:* **beak size of finches.**

**Stabilising selection** — **selection on common or intermediate forms of phenotypes, eliminating the extreme forms**, occurring **when individuals near the centre of the curve have higher fitness**.
*Example:* **selection on birth weight of infants.**

**Disruptive selection** — **selection on both extreme ends of phenotypes, eliminating the intermediate forms**, so **one population is divided into two distinct groups**. It occurs **when individuals at the outer ends of the curve have higher fitness than those near the middle**.
*Example:* **when the environment contains fewer medium-sized seeds, birds with small or large beaks have higher fitness.**

Each is defined by **where on the fitness curve the advantage lies** — one end, the middle, or both ends — which is the quickest way to tell them apart.

## Genetic drift

**Genetic drift** is **random genetic change in small populations**, where **alleles can become more or less common simply by chance**.

**Individuals with a particular allele may have more descendants than others just by chance**, and **over time a series of chance occurrences can cause an allele to become more or less common** in a population.

**Genetic bottleneck effect** — **a change in allele frequency following a dramatic reduction in the size of a population** due to a change in environment (disaster or disease). **Only a small portion of the population survives**, leading to a change in allele frequency. A disaster may kill many individuals, and **the survivors' gene pool contains different allele frequencies from the original**.

**The founder effect** — **a change in allele frequency that occurs when a few individuals from a population migrate to and colonise a new habitat**. **A few individuals become isolated from a larger population and establish a new one**, whose **allele frequency differs from the original population's**.

## Genetic equilibrium

**When a population is in genetic equilibrium — no evolution — allele frequencies remain constant.**

**Meiosis and fertilisation do not change allele frequency**, as they **neither produce new alleles nor select among them**. They **only create different combinations of alleles**.

## The Hardy–Weinberg principle

**Five conditions are required for genetic equilibrium:**

1. **Large population**
2. **No mutation**
3. **No sexual selection** (random mating)
4. **No migration**
5. **No natural selection**

$$p + q = 1, \qquad (p+q)^2 = 1, \qquad p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $p$ | Frequency of the **dominant** allele **A** |
| $q$ | Frequency of the **recessive** allele **a** |
| $p^2$ | Frequency of genotype **AA** |
| $2pq$ | Frequency of genotype **Aa** |
| $q^2$ | Frequency of genotype **aa** |

Each of the five conditions removes one cause of evolution, which is why a population violating any of them will be found to have changing allele frequencies.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Directional selection** | Selection on one extreme end of phenotypes |
| **Stabilising selection** | Selection on common or intermediate forms, eliminating extremes |
| **Disruptive selection** | Selection on both extreme ends, eliminating intermediates and dividing a population |
| **Genetic drift** | Random genetic change in small populations, where alleles shift by chance |
| **Genetic bottleneck effect** | A change in allele frequency after a dramatic reduction in population size |
| **Founder effect** | A change in allele frequency when a few individuals colonise a new habitat |
| **Genetic equilibrium** | A state of no evolution, in which allele frequencies remain constant |
| **Hardy–Weinberg principle** | The five conditions under which allele frequencies stay constant, and the equations describing them |

# 17.3 The Process of Speciation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Species and speciation

A **species** is **a population whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring**.

**Speciation** is **the formation of new species**.

## Reproductive isolation

**Reproductive isolation** is the **separation of populations so that they cannot reproduce**. It occurs **when members of two populations do not interbreed and produce fertile offspring**.

**1. Behavioural isolation** — two populations **develop differences in courtship rituals or other behaviours**.
*Examples:* **eastern and western meadowlarks use different songs to attract mates**; the blue-footed booby and the masked booby.

**2. Geographic isolation** — two populations are **separated by geographic barriers** such as rivers, mountains, or other bodies of water.
*Example:* **Abert's and Kaibab squirrels**, separated by the Grand Canyon.

Note the qualification the guide adds: **geographic barriers do not always guarantee isolation.**

**3. Temporal isolation** — **two or more species reproduce at different times**.
*Example:* **orchids blooming on different days.**

## Speciation in finches

The sequence: **founding of a new population → geographic isolation → changes in the new population's gene pool → behavioural isolation → ecological competition.**

**1. Founders arrive.** A few finches from mainland South America arrived on one of the Galápagos islands. Because of the **founder effect**, the **allele frequency of this population differs from the original**.

**2. Geographic isolation.** The combination of **founder effect, geographic isolation, and natural selection** enabled a new species (**Species A**). Later, a few birds from species A crossed to another island; because **these birds do not usually fly over open water**, they **move from island to island rarely** — geographic isolation.

**3. Changes in gene pool.** Over time, populations on each island **adapted to the local environment**, such as different types of food. **Natural selection caused two distinct populations to evolve (A and B)**, each characterised by a new phenotype.

**4. Behavioural isolation.** **Finches prefer to mate with birds that have same-sized beaks.** The **difference in beaks, combined with mating behaviour, produces reproductive isolation**. The **gene pools of the two populations remain isolated even when individuals live in the same place** — and the populations have become **two distinct species**.

Stage 4 is what makes the split permanent: geographic isolation ends when the birds meet again, behavioural isolation does not.

**5. Competition and continued evolution.** **More specialised birds have less competition for food.** Over time, **the differences between species increase, and new species evolve.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Species** | A population whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring |
| **Speciation** | The formation of new species |
| **Reproductive isolation** | The separation of populations so that they cannot reproduce |
| **Behavioural isolation** | Isolation from differences in courtship rituals or other behaviours |
| **Geographic isolation** | Isolation by geographic barriers such as rivers, mountains, or water |
| **Temporal isolation** | Isolation from species reproducing at different times |
| **Founder effect** | A differing allele frequency in a population founded by a few individuals |
