# S2M-1 Semester 2 Midterm review: 16.1-17.3

## Semester 2 Midterm review: 16.1-17.3

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Midterm Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Hannah Lai 9-9, Elisa Liu 9-10. Editor: Angela Ying 9-7. Range: 16.1-17.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

#### Chapter 16: Evolution

#### 16.1 Darwin’s Voyage of Discovery

Evolution

- The process of change over time
- Modern organisms evolved from common ancestors through descent over long periods of time
- Species: a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring

Charles Darwin

- 1st person to publish convincing evidences that species evolve
- Proposed reasonable mechanism explaining evolution (natural selection)
- Began 5 year voyage on HMS Beagle in 1831
  - To map coast of South America
  - Collected specimen of plants and animals, found evidences of evolution

3 Patterns of Biodiversity

- Species vary globally
  - Different species inhabit separate but ecologically similar habitats around the globe
  - i.e. similar flightless birds (ostrich, rhea, emu) inhabit separate but similar grasslands
- Species vary locally
  - Different species occupy different habitats within a local area
  - i.e. Isabela Island Tortoise vs Hood Island Tortoise
- Species vary overtime
  - Some fossils of extinct animals are similar to living species
    - fossils: preserved remains and traces of ancient organisms

Darwin’s thoughts

- Inspired by discoveries, especially in Galapagos Islands
- Wondered if species originated from common ancestor

#### 16.2 Ideas That Shaped Darwin’s Thinking

James Hulton

- Theory of Geological Change, 1785
  - Changes in Earth’s surface can be caused by slow and continuous changes
  - The Earth is much older than we once thought (thousands of years old)

Charles Lyell

- Principles of Geology
  - Geological processes in action today must be the same ones that shaped Earth millions of years ago
- Uniformitarianism: changes happening very gradually

Jean Baptiste Lamarck

- Hypothesis of the Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics, 1809
  - Acquired characteristics would be passed on to the offspring
    - Acquired characteristics: traits altered by an individual organism during its life by selectively using/disusing a body part
  - All organisms have an inborn urge to be more complex and perfect
- Evaluation of this hypothesis
  - Incorrect:
    - Evolution does not mean that over time a species becomes “better”
    - Acquired characteristics cannot be passed to offspring (only changes in reproduction cells can)
  - Correct:
    - One of the first naturalists to suggest that species changed
    - Among first to try to explain evolution scientifically using natural processes

Thomas Malthus

- Principle of populations, 1798
  - Wars, famine, and diseases limit population growth (population grows exponentially and these factors grow linearly)
  - If human population grows unchecked, not enough food/space

Artificial selection

- Nature provides variations, humans selectively breed those that are found useful
- Darwin realized some variations could be inherited
  - Natural variation – provides raw material for evolution

#### 16.3 Darwin Presents His Case

1859, Darwin, book “On the Origin of Species”

- Outlined ideas of evolution: natural selection with 3 principles

1. Struggle for existence

- If more individuals are produced than can survive, individuals must compete to abtain food, living space, and other limited necessities of life

2. Variation and adaptation

- Individuals in a population vary in heritable traits
- Adaptation: any heritable characteristic that increases an organism’s ability to survive and reproduce in its environment
  - i.e. camouflage, mimicry, certain behaviors

3. Survival of the fittest

- Fitness: how well an organism can survive and reproduce in its environment
  - Survive and reproduce always go together!!!
- Difference in the rates of survival and reproduction (passing hereditary adaptations on to the next generation)

Natural selection

- Process by which organisms with variations most suited to their local environment survive and leave more offsprings
  - Environment influences fitness
  - Well adapted individuals survive and reproduce

Common descent

- Over many generations, adaptations could cause successful species to evolve into new species
- Common descent: all species (living and extinct) are descended from ancient common ancestors
- Descent with modification: living species are descended with modification from common ancestors
  - Fossil records provide evidences of such descent

#### 16.4 Evidences of Evolution

Biogeography

- Study of where organisms live now and where they and their ancestors lived in the past
- Patterns in distribution of living and fossil species tell us how modern organisms evolved from their ancestors

Evolution Patterns

- Adaptive radiation: One species evolved into several different forms that live in different ways (closely related but different)
  - Adapted to different environments
  - Share common ancestors
  - i.e. Human and blue whale
- Convergent evolution: Unrelated organisms living in similar environments come to resemble each other (distantly related but similar)
  - Adapted to similar environments
  - Do not share common ancestors
  - i.e. Bat and bird (wings), shark and dolphin (fins)

Evidences of Evolution

- Fossils
  - Earth is 4.6 billion years old, enough timeframe for natural selection to happen
  - Intermediate fossil shows evolution of modern species from ancestors
    - Due to geological processes, marine fossils will be found on mountain tops
- Comparing anatomy
  - Homologous structures: similar structures in different species adapted for different functions
    - Evidence of recent common ancestor
    - i.e. forelimb in tetrapods (amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals)
  - Vestigial structure: structures inherited from ancestors which have lost much of their original functions due to different selection pressures on the descendant
    - A type of homologous structure
    - Evidence of common ancestor
    - i.e. hind limbs of whales and dolphins
  - Analogous structures: body parts that share a common function but not a common structure
    - Not evidence of common ancestor
    - i.e. wings of birds and bees
- Comparing embryology
  - Identifying similar patterns of embryo development
  - Evidence of common ancestor
  - i.e. all vertebrates exhibit similar structures in embryo development
    - Tail
    - Notochord (early form of a spine)
    - Pharyngeal pouches
- Genetic and molecular biology (most useful evidence)
  - Compare the genetic information of different species and determine whether they are closely related or not
  - All living things use the same genetic code
    - Comparing DNA/RNA/protein sequence is the most powerful evidence of common ancestry
  - Homologous genes
    - i.e. Hox genes
      - Determine the head to tail axis in embryonic development
      - In almost all multicellular organisms
      - Gene Hoxc8 most commonly looked at
  - Homologous proteins
    - i.e. Cytochrome C
      - Functions in cellular respiration
      - In almost all living cells

Testing natural selection

- Darwin’s hypothesis: natural selection shaped the beaks of different bird populations as they become adapted to eating different foods
- The Grants observed the Galápagos finches living in their natural environment to evaluate Darwin’s hypothesis
  - 2 assumptions
    - For beak size and shape to evolve, there must be enough heritable variations in those traits
    - Differences in beak size and shape must produce difference in fitness
  - Conclusion: variation within a species increases the likelihood of the species’ adapting to and surviving environment change

#### Chapter 17: Evolution of Populations

#### 17.1 Genes and variation

Gregor Mendel

- Born in 1822, Germany; Botanist
- He tested 34 varieties for constancy of their traits. He chose seven traits, such as plant height (short or tall) and seed color (green or yellow)

Genetics

- The scientific study of heredity
  - Heredity: delivery of traits from parent to offspring
- Terms
  - Traits
    - A specific feature inherited from the parents
    - Physical / physiological / behavioral characteristics
    - Determined by genes
    - A trait many have different forms
  - Genes
    - Basic unit of heredity, determine traits
    - Specific fragment of DNA on chromosomes
  - Alleles
    - Different forms of a gene
    - Determine different forms of one trait
    - Differ from each other by one or a few DNA bases only
  - Gene pool
    - All the genes, including all the different alleles for each gene present in a population
  - Allele frequency
    - The number of times a particular allele occurs in a gene pool
  - Homologous chromosomes
    - Pair of chromosomes that one comes from the male parent and one from the female parent
      - Same genes in same order, same length, same shape
      - May not the same alleles for one gene
  - Genotype
    - Particular combination of alleles an organism carries
    - Together with environmental conditions, determine its traits
    - Homozygous: same alleles on the homologous chromosomes
    - Heterozygous: different alleles on the homologous chromosomes
  - Phenotype (same thing as traits)
    - All physical, physiological, and behavioral characteristics of an organism

Genetics Joins Evolutionary Theory

- Heritable traits are controlled by genes that are carried on chromosomes
- Mutation in genes generate various forms of alleles, hence generate variation
- Natural selection acts directly on phenotype, not genotype
- Evolution is any change in the relative frequency of alleles in the gene pool of a population overtime
  - Natural selection operates on individuals, but ultimately changes allele frequencies in the gene pool, so populations evolve

Sources of Genetic Variation

- Mutation
  - Any change in the genetic material of a cell
    - Gene mutation, chromosome mutation
  - Beneficial, neutral, harmful (most are neutral)
  - Only mutations in germ line cells that produce gametes can be passed on to offsprings
- Sexual Reproduction
  - Meiosis (crossing over and independent assortment of homologous chromosomes)
    - Crossing over: paired chromosomes swap lengths of DNA at random
    - Independent assortment: the random arrangement and separation of homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis
  - Sexual reproduction increases genetic variation without changing allele frequency!!
  - Fertilization of sperm and egg
- Lateral Gene transfer
  - Organisms pass genes from one individual to another that is not its offspring
    - Can occur between same or different species
    - Increase genetic variation in a species
    - i.e. Bacterial conjugation

Single-Gene and Polygenic Traits

- The number of phenotypes produced for a trait depends on how many genes control the trait
- Single-Gene Traits
  - A trait controlled by only one gene
  - May have just 2-4 distinct phenotypes
  - i.e. pea plant flower color is controlled by only gene, with two alleles
  - i.e. Human ABO blood type is controlled by one gene, with three alleles
- Polygenic traits
  - Traits controlled by two or more genes
  - The trait shows wide range (usually continuous) phenotypes
  - Also influenced by environmental factors
  - Distribution of phenotype tend to show normal distribution
  - i.e. Human skin color

#### 17.2 Evolution as Genetic Change in Populations

1. Natural selection on single-gene traits

  - Selection on particular phenotype Change in allele frequency Evolution

2. Natural selection on polygenetic traits

  - Selection on a range of phenotypes Change in allele frequency Evolution
- Directional selection
  - Selection on one extreme end of phenotypes
    - When individuals at one end of the curve have higher fitness than individuals in the middle or the other end
    - i.e. Beak size of finches
- Stabilizing selection
  - Selection on common or intermediate forms of phenotypes, eliminating extreme forms
    - When individuals near the center of the curve have higher fitness than the individuals at two ends
    - i.e. Selection on birth weights of infants
- Disruptive selection
  - Selection on both extreme ends of phenotypes, eliminating common groups
    - One population divides into two distinct groups
    - When individuals at the two ends of the curve have higher fitness that the individuals near the center
    - i.e. Decrease of medium sized seeds leads to
      - Birds with usually small or large beaks would have higher fitness
      - Two groups: One with smaller beaks and one with larger beaks

3. Genetic Drift

- Alleles can become more or less common by chance
- Random change in allele frequency
- Usually in small populations
- Individuals carrying a particular allele may leave more descendants than others
- BY CHANCE
  - Bottleneck effect
    - A change in allele frequency following a dramatic reduction in the size of the population
      - Due to change in the environment (disaster, disease)
      - Only a small portion of the population survived
      - Leading to a change in allele frequency
  - Founder effect
    - A change in allele frequency that may occur when a few individuals from a population migrate to and colonize a new habitat
      - Due to migration of a small subgroup of a population
      - Few individuals become isolated from a large population and establish a new population
      - The new population's allele frequency is different from the original population’s

Evolution vs. Genetic Equilibrium

- A population is in genetic equilibrium or not evolving if allele frequencies don’t change
  - Only for a short period of time
- Hardy Weinberg principle, five conditions are required for genetic equilibrium
  - A large population: genetic drift has less effect on large populations than on small populations.
  - No mutations: no new alleles be introduced into the gene pool.
  - No sexual selection (random mating): All members of the population must have an equal opportunity to produce offspring.
  - No migration (no gene flow): Population does not gain or lose alleles by any movement of individuals into or out of a population.
  - No natural selection: No phenotype can have a selective advantage over another.
- The Hardy-Weinberg Equation
  - p=frequency of allele A (dominant allele)
  - q=frequency of allele a (recessive allele)
  - p+q=1, (p+q)2=1 so p2+2pq+ q2=1
  - p2=frequency of AA (homozygous dominant)
  - 2pq =frequency of Aa (heterozygous)
  - q2=frequency of aa (homozygous recessive)

## 17.3 The Process of Speciation

Isolating Mechanisms

- Speciation: the formation of a new species.
- Reproductive isolation: separation of population so that they do not recognize each other for mating purposes
  - Three types:
    - Behavioral isolation
      - Two populations develop different in courtship (seeking affections) rituals, or other behaviors.
      - i.e. eastern and western meadow larks use different songs to attract mates.
    - Geographic isolation
      - Two populations are separated by geographic barriers such as rivers, mountains, or bodies of water.
      - i.e. Abert's and kaibab squirrels
      - Geographic barriers do not always guarantee isolation. (think about birds when writing the exam!)
    - Temporal isolation
      - Two or more species reproduce at different times.
      - i.e. orchids bloom on different days.
      - Premating mechanisms vs postmating mechanism

Case Study: Speciation in Darwin’s Finches

- Speciation in Galapagos finches occurred by founding of a new population, geographic isolation, changes in the new population’s gene pool, behavioral isolation, and ecological competition.

# S2F-1 16.3 Darwin Presents his Case

## 16.3 Darwin Presents his Case

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Clover 9-12, Erica Zhang 9-7. Editor: Jun Lee 9-5. Range: 16.3-19.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

-Jean-Baptiste Lamarck: ideas on the inheritance of acquired characteristics had been ridiculed by scientists, including some of Darwin’s own teachers.

-Alfred Russell Wallace: English naturalist who wrote an essay in Malaysia with ideas on evolution almost identical to Darwin’s, which was presented alongside Darwin’s observations at an 1858 scientific meeting

-Charles Darwin: worked out the main points of natural selection after reading Malthus, but did not publish for 20 years; after reviewing Wallace’s essay in 1858, he published On the Origin of Species in 1859

**Evolution by Natural Selection**

-In On the Origin of Species, he combined his own thoughts with ideas from Malthus and Lamarck.

- The Struggle of Existence

-if more individuals are produced than can survive, members of a population must compete to obtain food, living space, and other limited necessities of life

- Variation and Adaptation

-individuals in a population vary in heritable characteristics, and Darwin hypothesized that some of those variants are better suited to life in their environment than others

-Adaptation: any heritable characteristic that increases an organism’s ability to survive and reproduce in its environment

- Mimicry: an adaptation in which an organism copies or mimics a more dangerous organism (Batesian mimicry)
- Camouflage: an adaptation that allows an organism to blend into its background and avoid predation
- Behaviors
- Survival of the Fittest

-Fitness: how well an organism can survive and reproduce in its environment

-Survival of the Fittest: the difference in rates of survival and reproduction

-Survival (in evolutionary terms): reproducing and passing adaptations on to the next generation

- Natural Selection

-the process by which organisms with variations most suited to their local environment survive and leave more offspring

-occurs in situation in which more individuals are born than can survive(the struggle for existence), there is natural heritable variation(variation and adaptation), and their various fitness among individuals(survival of the fittest)

- Case Study: Peppered Moth (Biston betularia)

-environmental pressure: predation by birds

-variation: black and white moth; white moth are common before industrial revolution because they are camouflaged against white lichen on trees

-environmental change: during the industrial revolution, pollution from factories darken the tree trunks

-result: white moth decline due to predation; black moth is camouflaged by black soot, black moth increases

- Case Study: Antibiotic Resistance

-the resistance of bacterium to an antibiotic that was originally effective for treatment of infections caused by it

- In high number of bacteria, few are resistant to antibiotics
- Antibiotics kill bacteria causing the illness and good bacteria protecting the body from infection
- The resistant bacteria now have preferred conditions to grow and take over
- Bacteria can even transfer their drug resistance to other bacteria through lateral gene transfer, causing more problems

Natural Selection vs. Evolution

-often used interchangeably

-natural selection is a mechanism of evolution, organisms can evolve in other ways

**Common Descent**

-over many generations, adaptation could cause successful species to evolve into new species

-descent with modification: living species are descended, with modification, from common ancestors

-fossil records provide for evidence – intermediate fossils forms show evolution of modern species from ancestors

-all species--living and extinct--are descended from the same ancient common ancestor

## 16.4 Evidence of Evolution

**Biogeography**

-the study of where organisms live now and where they and their ancestors lived in the past

-patterns in the distribution of living and fossil tell how modern organisms evolved from their ancestors

**Geographic Distribution of Species**

- Closely Related but Different (adaptive radiation)

-one species evolved into several different forms that live in different ways

-adapt to different environments and share a common ancestor

- Distantly Related but similar (convergent evolution)

-unrelated organisms live in similar environment and come to resemble on another

-adapt to similar environment and don’t share a common ancestor

**Comparing Anatomy and Embryology**

- Homologous Structures

-structures that are shared by related species and that have been inherited from a common ancestor

-evidence of common ancestor

-different species have structure adapted for different function but these structures show many similarities

-similarities and differences among homologous structures help determine how recently species shared a common ancestor

- Analogous Structures

-body parts that share a common function, but not common structure

-don’t provide evidence of common ancestor

- Vestigial Structures

-structures that are inherited from ancestors, but have lost much of their original function due to different selection pressures on the descendant

-evidence of common ancestors

- Comparing Embryology

-similar patterns of embryological development provide further evidence that organisms have descended from a common ancestor

-e.g. all vertebrate embryos exhibit common structures: a tail, a notochord, and pharyngeal pouches

**The Age of Earth and Fossils**

- The Age of Earth

-evolution requires a very old Earth because it takes a long time; if life has evolved, then our planet must be billions of years old.

-radioactive dating shows Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, giving evolution by natural selection time to happen.

- Recent Fossil Finds

-fossils: preserved or mineralized remains or imprints of an organisms that lived long ago

-many recently discovered fossils form series that trace the evolution of modern species from extinct ancestors

**Genetics and Molecular Biology**

-all living organisms use the same universal genetic code

-similarities in DNA/RNA protein sequences provide the most powerful evidence of common ancestors

- Homologous genes help to determine the head to tail axis in embryonic development

-homologous hox genes are found in almost all multicellular animals

- Homologous proteins function in cellular respiration

-similar versions of cytochrome c are found in almost all living cells

- Testing Natural Selection

-the Grants’ data also confirm factors that drive natural selection

-competition/overproduction

-environmental change

-sexual reproduction

# S2F-2 17.1 Genes and Variation

## 17.1 Genes and Variation

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Clover 9-12, Erica Zhang 9-7. Editor: Jun Lee 9-5. Range: 16.3-19.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Genetics Joins Evolutionary Theory**

**Gregor Mendel:** scientist that discovered the basic laws of heredity through experiments with pea plants

- “Father of Genetics”

**Genetics:** the scientific study of heredity

- **Heredity:** delivery of traits from parent to offspring

**Alleles:** specific forms of a gene that may vary individual to individual

- **dominant allele**: allele that is expressed in an organism's appearance even when only one copy is present.
- **recessive allele**: allele that is expressed only when two copies are present and no dominant allele is present.

**Genotype:** specific combination of alleles an organism carries

- **Homozygous:** same alleles on the homologous chromosomes
- **Heterozygous:** different alleles on the homologous chromosomes

**Phenotype:** all physical, physiological, and behavioral characteristics of an organism

- natural selection acts directly on phenotype (not genotype!)

**Trait**: characteristic or feature of an organism

(To differ between phenotype, genotype, allele, and trait: eg. flower color is a trait, purple flowers is a phenotype, Pp is a genotype, and P is a dominant allele)

**Natural Selection:**

- Mutations in genes generate various forms of alleles (variation)
- Natural selection acts directly on phenotypes, not genotype
- some individuals have phenotypes that are better suited to their environment than others
- these individuals are more likely to survive and reproduce (more likely to pass on more copies of their genes to others)

**Population**: group of individuals of same species that can interbreed

**Gene pool**: all the genes and alleles present in a population

**Allele frequency**: number of times an allele occurs in a gene pool

- Has nothing to do with whether an allele is dominant or recessive

**Evolution:** (in genetic terms) the change of allele in a population over time.

- unlike natural selection, populations evolve, not individuals

**Sources of Genetic Variation**

**Mutation:** any change in genetic material of a cell

- neutral mutations: do not change organism’s phenotype
- May increase, decrease, or not affect fitness
- Only mutations in gametes would be passed to the next generation

**Genetic Recombination During Sexual Reproduction:**

- during independent assortment, chromosomes move independently, producing unique gene combinations that make the next generation different from its parents
- During crossing over, paired chromosomes swap DNA randomly
- Sexual reproduction increases genetic variation without changing the allele frequency

**Lateral Gene Transfer:** passing of genes from one organism to another organisms that’s not its offspring

- genes can be passed to same or other species
- increases genetic variation in species that receives the new genes
- eg. Bacteria swap genes on plasmids in the evolution of antibiotic resistance

**Single-Gene and Polygenic Traits**

- number of phenotypes produced for a trait depends on how many genes control the trait

**Single-gene trait**: trait controlled by one gene

- usually, there’s only 2-4 distinct phenotypes
- eg. human ABO blood type

**Polygenic trait**: trait controlled by two or more genes

- many possible genotypes and phenotypes
- eg. human height
- **normal distribution**: bell-shaped curve that appears when many genes contribute small effects to the same trait

## 17.2 Evolution as Genetic Change in Populations

**How Natural Selection Works**

**Evolutionary fitness**: success in passing genes to the next generation

**Evolutionary adaptation**: any genetically controlled trait that increases individual’s ability to pass along it alleles

**Natural Selection on single-gene traits**: selection on particular phenotype -> changes in allele frequency -> changes in phenotype frequencies -> evolution

**Natural selection on polygenic traits**: selection on a range of phenotypes -> changes in allele frequency -> changes in phenotype frequencies -> 3 types of selection: directional, stabilizing, disruptive

**Directional Selection:** individuals at one end of the curve have higher fitness than individuals in the middle/at the other end

- eg. Beak sizes of Galapagos finches

**Stabilizing Selection**: individuals near the center of the curve have higher fitness than individuals at either end

- intermediate organisms have higher fitness
- Eg. Birth weights of infants

**Disruptive selection**: individuals at outer ends of the curve have higher fitness than individuals near the middle

- acts against intermediate organisms
- Eg. In particular bird population with disruptive selection, the population might split into two groups: one with smaller beaks and one with larger beaks

**Genetic Drift**: random change in allele frequency

- individuals that carry a particular allele may leave more descendants than other individuals by chance
- **Bottleneck** **Effect**: change in allele frequency following a dramatic reduction in the size of a population
- Eg. A disease/disaster that kills many individuals in the population, and by random chance, the remaining population’s gene pool may contain different allele frequencies
- **Founder Effect**: allele frequencies change as a result of the migration of a small subgroup of population, new population’s allele frequency doesn’t reflect old group’s
- Eg. Fruit flies on Hawaiian islands descended from same mainland fruit fly population, but they have different allele frequencies from the original

**Evolution VS Genetic Equilibrium**

**Genetic Equilibrium**: population is not evolving, allele frequencies in its gene pool do not change

- Meiosis and fertilization (during sexual reproduction) do not change allele frequencies! (But increase genetic diversity, as mentioned in 17.1). Hypothetically, population of sexually reproducing organisms could remain in genetic equilibrium.

-

**Hardy-Weinberg Principle:** allele frequencies should remain constant unless one or more of factors cause those frequencies to change (five factors listed below)

- **Nonrandom mating**: organisms in the population do not have equal opportunity to produce offspring
- **A small population:** genetic drift have deadly effect on small populations
- **Immigration/emigration:** causes **gene flow**, which introduces/takes away alleles to a population
- **Mutations:** introduce new alleles in gene pool
- **Natural Selection**: different genotypes have different fitness, driving evolution

**Hardy Weinberg Equation:**

- p+q=1, (p+q)2=1
- p = frequency of dominant allele (A) , q = frequency of recessive allele (a)
- p2=frequency of homozygous dominant (AA), 2pq =frequency of heterozygous (Aa), q2=frequency of homozygous recessive (aa)

## 17.3 The Process of Speciation

**Isolating Mechanisms**

**Species**: a population or group of populations whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring

**Speciation**: formation of a new species

**Reproductive** **isolation**: when members of a population stop breeding with other members, over time, isolated gene pools diverge into separate species.

**Behavioral isolation:** two populations develop differences in courtship rituals/other behaviors

    - Eg. Eastern and western meadowlarks, which won’t mate each other since they use different songs to attract males
  - **Geographic isolation**: two populations separated by geographic barriers such as rivers/mountains
    - Eg. Abert’s squirrel, where a small population became isolated on the north rim of the Grand Canyon, forming separate gene pools than the major population, and over time, evolving differently into two separate species
    - Geographic barriers do not always guarantee isolation.
      - Eg. large river can separate animals on land, but cannot separate bird populations
- **Temporal Isolation:** two or more species reproduce at different times
    - Pre-mating/post-mating mechanism
    - Eg. Similar species of orchids bloom on different days, so they can’t pollinate each other

**Speciation in Darwin’s Finches**

**Peter and Rosemary Grant:**

- hypothesis: speciation in Galapagos finches occurred by founder effect -> geographic isolation -> changes in the new population’s gene pool -> behavioral isolation -> ecological competition -> speciation(s) (Refer to the textbook for specific explanations)

## 18.1 Finding Order in Diversity

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Clover 9-12, Erica Zhang 9-7. Editor: Jun Lee 9-5. Range: 16.3-19.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Assigning Scientific Names**

- Common names can be confusing, as they vary among languages and in different places
- Eg. Buzzard refers to hawk in UK but refers to a vulture in US

**Dichotomous (single-access) Key**: tool used to identify organisms by making a series of choices between two contrasting characteristics

**Binomial Nomenclature:** two-word naming system in where each species is assigned a two-part scientific name

  - By Carolus Linnaeus, 1730s, Swedish
  - The first part (capital) is the genus the organisms belongs to, second part (lowercase) is unique to each species (Italics, underline in handwriting)
  - **Genus:** group of similar species

**Systematics**: science of naming and grouping organisms

  - goal of systematics: organize living things into groups called taxa that have biological meaning

**The Linnaean Classification System**

  - 7 hierarchical taxa: **Kingdom > phylum > class > order > family > genus > species**

**Problems with Traditional Classification:**

  - based on **morphology** (form and structure) similarity and difference
  - classifying organisms by visible similarities and differences seem simple, but how to determine which is the most important?
  - Only species in the 7 hierarchical taxa is a “natural” definition (since species is defined by whether organisms can mate each other and produce fertile offspring)

## 18.2 Modern Evolutionary Classification

**Evolutionary Classification**

**Evolution**: descent with modification

**Phylogeny**: evolutionary history of lineages

  - **Lineages**: evolutionary lines

**Phylogenetics systematics**: (aka evolutionary classification)

- goal: to group species into categories that reflect lines of evolutionary descent, rather than overall similarities and differences
- Organisms grouped based on how recently they share a common ancestor
- **Clade**: group of species that includes single common ancestor and all descendants
  - **Cladistics:** method of classifying species of organisms into clades
  - Many traditional taxonomic groups do form valid clades, but many don’t
    - Eg. Linnean class Reptilla excludes birds, so class Reptilla is not clade Reptilla.
- **Monophyletic group**: single common ancestor and all its descendants (eg. Clade)
- **Paraphyletic group**: common ancestor but excludes one or more group of descendants
    - invalid evolutionary classification

**Cladograms**

**Cladogram**: tree diagram that links groups of organisms by showing how lineages branched off from common ancestors

  - Bottom (root): common ancestor shared by all organisms on the cladogram
  - Branching points (nodes): denote speciation
  - Patterns indicate degrees of relatedness among organisms
  - **Ingroup**: group of organisms on cladogram that are being studied and share a more recent common ancestor with each other
  - **Outgroup**: organism or group that is closely related to the in-group but branched off earlier and is used as a reference point for comparison

**Derived character**: trait that arose in most recent common ancestor of particular lineage clade and was passed along its descendants

  - absence of a trait isn’t used as derived character, since distantly related groups of organisms can lose the same character

**Primital (ancestral) character**: character possessed by members of particular clade but that evolved before branching of clade defined

**DNA in Classification**

**Genetics**: primary basis for grouping organisms to clades and determining likely paths of evolutionary descent

- use of DNA in cladistics analysis has helped to make evolutionary trees more accurate
- Since all genes mutate over time, shared gene contains differences that can be treated as derived characters in cladistics analysis. So, similarities and differences in DNA can be used to develop hypotheses about evolutionary relationships.

**In general, more derived genetic characters two species share, more recently they shared common ancestor, and more closely they’re related in evolutionary terms.**

## 18.3 Building the Tree of Life

**Six Kingdoms: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, “Protista”, Eubacteria, Archaebacteria**

**Cell Types: Prokaryote (**原核生物**), Eukaryote (**真核生物**)**

**Cell Number: Uni/Multicellular**

**Mode of Nutrition: Auto/Heterotroph**

  - **Autrotrophic modes of nutrition: photosynthesis/chemosynthesis**

**Oxygen use: Aerobic/Anaerobic**

**Cell Structure: Cell wall (peptidoglycan, cellulose, chitin) / chloroplast - chlorophyll**

- By 1990s, researchers realized eubacteria and archaebacteria in Monera where genetically and biochemically different, so, monera was separated into two.

**Domain:** larger, more inclusive category than a kingdom.

- **Bacteria, Archaea, Eukaryota**

**The Tree of All Life**

**The Tree of Life:** shows current hypothesis regarding evolutionary relationships among taxa within 3 domains of life

**Domain Archaea:** lives in extreme environments; may oblige to anaerobic conditions

**Domain Eukarya:** has a nucleus

  - **Animalia:** usually mobile, **Plantae**: usually nonmobile
  - **“Protista”:** paraphyletic, some display characteristics that resemble animals, plants, and fungi (since it’s paraphyletic, it is considered invalid evolutionary classification, thus it has “”)

## 19.1 The Fossil Record

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Clover 9-12, Erica Zhang 9-7. Editor: Jun Lee 9-5. Range: 16.3-19.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Fossils and Ancient Life**

-fossils: the preserved remains/traces of ancient life

-from fossil record, paleontologists learn about the structure of ancient organisms, their environment, and the ways in which they lived

-specific conditions are needed for fossilization

-only tiny % of living things become fossils

Types of Fossils

- Petrified Fossils: minerals replace all/part of an organism
- Trace Fossils: evidence of the activities of ancient organisms, such as footprint burrow
- Mold: hollow area in sediment in the shape of an organism/part of an organisms
- Cast: copy of the shape of an organism

-other fossils form when the remains of organisms are preserved in substances such as tar, amber, or ice

-amber preserved fossils: organisms that become trapped in tree resin that hardens after the tree is buried

-preserved remains form when an entire organism becomes encased in materials such as ice

Fossils in Sedimentary Rock

**Dating Earth’s History**

- Relative Dating

-places rock layers and their fossils into a temporal sequence

-allows paleontologists to determine whether a fossil is older or younger than other fossils

-Index fossils: distinctive fossils used to establish and compare the relative ages of rock layers and the fossil they contain

-existed only in a few layers (during specific spans of time)

-occured in large geographic areas

-include trilobites

- Radiometric Dating

-relies on radioactive isotopes, which decay, or breakdown, into stable isotopes at a steady rate

-compares the amount of radioactive to nonradioactive isotopes in a sample to determine its age

-half life: time required for half of radioactive atoms in a sample to decay

-Carbon-14: 5730 years

**Geologic Time Scale**

-timeline of Earth’s history

-based on both relative and absolute dating

**Life on a Changing Planet**

- Physical Forces

-building mountains, opening coastlines, changing climates, and geological forces have altered habitats of living organisms repeatedly through Earth history

-the theory of a plate tectonic explains how solid continental plates move slowly above Earth’s molten core--continental drift

-forces from space have even altered Earth’s physical environment

-strong evidence: comets and meteors have crashed into Earth many times in the past

- Biological Forces

-first photosynthesis organisms began absorbing carbon dioxide and releasing large amounts of oxygen

-actions of living organisms over time have changed conditions in the land, water, and atmosphere of Earth

## 19.2 Pattern and Process of Evolution

**Speciation and Extinction**

-macroevolution: grand transformation in anatomy, phylogeny, ecology, and behavior, which usually take place in clades larger than a single species

-speciation of larger clades

-extinction of larger clades

-microevolution: the change in allele frequency that occurs over time within a population

- Macroevolution and Cladistics

-fossils are classified using the cladistic techniques, based on shared derived characteristics, that are used to classify living species

-in some cases, fossils are placed in clades that contain only extinct organisms; in other cases, fossils are classified into clades that include living organisms

- Adaptation and Extinction

-if rate of speciation in a clade >= rate of extinction, the clade continue to exist

-if rate of extinction in a clade >= rate of speciation, the clade eventually become extinct

- Patterns of Extinction

-background extinction

-extinct because of the slow but steady process of natural selection

-mass extinction

-extinct over relatively short period of time

-entire ecosystem vanish

-whole food web collapse

-natural selection can’t compensate quickly

-factors include volcanic eruptions, moving continents, changing sea levels

**Rate of Evolution**

-evidence shows that evolution has often proceeded at different rates for different organisms at different times over the long history of life on Earth

- Gradualism

-Darwin

-evolution occured by a long sequence of continuous change

-species slowly change through a series of intermediate forms

-lack of intermediates--incomplete fossil record

- Punctuated Equilibrium

-Stephen J Gould and Niles Eidrege

-long periods of relative stability in a species are punctuated by periods of rapid evolution

-no long sequence of intermediate forms

**Adaptive Radiation and Convergent Evolution**

- Adaptive Radiation

-single species evolves over a relatively short time into several different forms that live in different ways

-species display variations on the ancestral body plan

-occupy different ecological niches

- Convergent Evolution

-groups of organisms evolve in different places at different times, but similar environments

-organisms face similar selection pressure

-produces similar structures and characteristics

-emus, rheas, ostriches

**Coevolution**

-two species evolve in response to changes in each other over time

- flowers and pollinators:
- orchid with long spur and moth with long feeding tube
- plants and herbivorous insects:

-plant evolve bad tasting or poisonous compounds

-insects evolved variants that could alter, inactive, or eliminate poisons

## 2.2 Properties of Water

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Oscar 9-1. Range: 2.2, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**The Water Molecule**

  - **Polarity:** A water molecule (H₂O) is **polar** because the oxygen atom is more electronegative, pulling the shared electrons closer. This creates a slightly negative oxygen end and slightly positive hydrogen ends.

**Hydrogen Bonding**

  - The attraction between the positive hydrogen end of one water molecule and the negative oxygen end of another.
  - Though individually weak, the multitude of hydrogen bonds gives water its unique properties.

**Key Properties of Water:**

  - **Cohesion:** The attraction between molecules of the same substance (water to water). Explains **surface tension** (e.g., insects walking on water).
  - **Adhesion:** The attraction between molecules of different substances (e.g., water to glass). Explains **capillary action** (e.g., water moving up a plant's roots and stems) and the **meniscus** in a graduated cylinder.
  - **Heat Capacity:** Water can absorb or release a large amount of heat with only a small temperature change. This helps regulate cell temperatures and stabilizes environmental temperatures (e.g., in oceans).

**The pH Scale**

  - Measures the concentration of Hydrogen ions (H⁺) in a solution.
  - Ranges from 0 to 14.
  - **pH 7 = Neutral** (equal H⁺ and OH⁻ ions). Pure water is neutral.
  - **pH below 7 = Acidic** (more H⁺ ions). The lower the pH, the stronger the acid.
  - **pH above 7 = Basic (Alkaline)** (more OH⁻ ions). The higher the pH, the stronger the base.
  - Each step on the scale represents a tenfold change in H⁺ ion concentration.

**Acids and Bases**

  - **Acid:** A compound that forms H⁺ ions in solution (e.g., HCl, lemon juice).
  - **Base:** A compound that forms OH⁻ ions in solution (e.g., NaOH, soap).

**Buffers**

  - Weak acids or bases that can react with strong acids or bases to prevent sharp, sudden changes in pH.
  - **Crucial for maintaining homeostasis** in organisms. For example, blood has buffers (bicarbonate) to keep its pH stable at around 7.4.

**3.1 Introduction to Ecology.**

**What is Ecology?**

  - **Ecology** is the scientific study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical environment.
  - The **biosphere** is the combined portions of the planet where all life exists, including land, water, and air.

**Levels of Organization**

  - Ecologists study nature at different levels, from an individual to the entire planet:
  - **Species:** A group of similar organisms that can breed and produce fertile offspring.
  - **Population:** A group of individuals of the same species that live in the same area.
  - **Community:** An assemblage of different populations that live together in a defined area.
  - **Ecosystem:** All the organisms that live in a place, together with their physical environment.
  - **Biome:** A group of ecosystems that share similar climates and typical organisms.
  - **Biosphere:** Our entire planet, with all its organisms and physical environments.

**Biotic and Abiotic Factors**

- An **ecosystem** is shaped by the combination of its **biotic** (living) and **abiotic** (non-living) factors.
- **Biotic factors** include any living part of the environment with which an organism might interact (animals, plants, fungi, bacteria).
- **Abiotic factors** include any nonliving part of the environment (sunlight, heat, precipitation, humidity, wind, water currents, soil type).
- Key Concept: These factors are **interdependent**. For example, a forest (biotic) affects the humidity and soil (abiotic) of an area.

**Ecological Methods**

- Ecologists use **three** main scientific approaches:
- **Observation**: The first step; asking questions, often leading to experiments or models.
- **Experimentation**: Testing hypotheses in a lab or field setting.
- **Modeling**: Using mathematical formulas based on data to understand complex, long-term phenomena.

# S1M-2 3.2 Energy, Producers, and Consumers

## 3.2 Energy, Producers, and Consumers

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Oscar 9-1. Range: 2.2, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Primary Producers (Autotrophs)**

- Autotrophs use solar or chemical energy to produce their own "food" by converting inorganic compounds into complex organic molecules (like carbohydrates).
- They are called **primary producers** because they store energy in forms that become available to other organisms. They are the foundation of all ecosystems.
- **Photosynthesis**: Captures light energy to power reactions that convert CO₂ and water into oxygen and energy-rich carbohydrates. (Plants, algae, some bacteria).
- **Chemosynthesis**: Uses chemical energy (from hydrogen sulfide) to produce carbohydrates. Found in deep-sea vents, hot springs, and other extreme environments.

**Consumers (Heterotrophs)**

- Heterotrophs must **acquire energy** from other organisms by ingesting them.
- Types of Consumers:
  - **Carnivores**: Kill and eat other animals (e.g., snakes, lions).
  - **Scavengers**: Consume dead carcasses of animals killed by predators or that died naturally (e.g., vultures).
  - **Herbivores**: Eat plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits (e.g., cows, caterpillars).
  - **Omnivores**: Have diets that naturally include both plants and animals (e.g., humans, bears).
  - **Decomposers**: "Feed" by chemically breaking down organic matter, returning nutrients to the soil (e.g., bacteria, fungi).
  - **Detritivores**: Feed on detritus (small pieces of decaying plant and animal remains) by chewing or grinding it into smaller pieces (e.g., earthworms, snails).

## 3.3 Energy Flow in Ecosystems

**Food Chains and Food Webs**

  - Energy flows through an ecosystem in a **one-way stream**, from primary producers to various consumers.
  - A **food chain** is a series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by eating and being eaten (e.g., algae → small fish → large fish → bird).
  - A **food web** is a network of complex, interconnected feeding relationships formed from all the food chains in an ecosystem. It shows that most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one species.
  - Key Concept: **Decomposers and detritivores** are essential as they recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem for use by primary producers.

**Trophic Levels and Ecological Pyramids**

  - Each step in a food chain or web is called a **trophic level**.
    - **First trophic level:** Primary Producers
    - **Second trophic level:** Primary Consumers (Herbivores)
    - **Third trophic level:** Secondary Consumers (Carnivores that eat herbivores)
    - **Fourth trophic level:** Tertiary Consumers (Carnivores that eat other carnivores)
  - **Ecological pyramids** show the relative amount of energy or matter contained within each trophic level.

**Pyramids of Energy:**

    - Show that the amount of energy available decreases at each succeeding trophic level.
    - On average, only about **10%** of the energy from one trophic level is transferred to the next. The rest is used for life processes (respiration, movement) or lost as heat.
    - This 10% rule explains why there are typically fewer organisms at higher trophic levels and why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.
  - **Pyramids of Biomass:** Illustrate the relative amount of living organic matter (biomass) at each trophic level.
  - **Pyramids of Numbers:** Show the relative number of individual organisms at each trophic level.

## 3.4 Cycles of Matter

**Biogeochemical Cycles**

  - Unlike energy, matter is recycled within and between ecosystems.
  - Elements pass from one organism to another and through the environment through closed loops called **biogeochemical cycles**.
  - These cycles involve biological, geological, and chemical processes.

**The Water Cycle**

  - Water moves between the oceans, atmosphere, and land.
  - Key Processes:
    - **Evaporation:** Water turning from liquid to vapor (from oceans, lakes).
    - **Transpiration:** Water vapor released by plants.
    - **Condensation:** Water vapor forming clouds.
    - **Precipitation:** Water falling as rain, snow, etc.
    - **Runoff:** Water flowing over land into rivers and oceans.
    - **Groundwater:** Water seeping into the soil.

**The Carbon Cycle**

  - Carbon is a key component of all organic compounds.
  - Key Processes:
    - **Biological:** Photosynthesis (takes in CO₂), Cellular Respiration (releases CO₂), Decomposition.
    - **Geochemical:** Release of CO₂ by volcanoes, burial and conversion of dead organisms into fossil fuels (coal, oil) over millions of years.
    - **Human Activity:** Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests releases large amounts of CO₂ into the atmosphere.

**The Nitrogen Cycle**

  - All organisms need nitrogen to make proteins and nucleic acids.
  - Although nitrogen gas (N₂) makes up 78% of the atmosphere, most organisms cannot use it in this form.
  - Key Processes:
    - **Nitrogen Fixation:** Certain types of bacteria convert N₂ gas into ammonia (NH₃). This occurs in soil and on roots of legumes (e.g., peanuts, peas).
    - **Assimilation:** Plants absorb nitrogen compounds (ammonia, nitrates) from the soil and incorporate them into proteins. Consumers get nitrogen by eating producers.
    - **Decomposition:** Decomposers return nitrogen to the soil as ammonia.
    - **Denitrification:** Other bacteria convert nitrates in the soil back into N₂ gas, which returns to the atmosphere.

**The Phosphorus Cycle**

  - Phosphorus is essential for DNA and RNA.
  - Unlike other cycles, it does **not** include the atmosphere. It is found mainly in rock, soil minerals, and ocean sediments.
  - It is released slowly as rocks wear down and is cycled locally between organisms and the soil.

**Nutrient Limitation**

  - **Primary Productivity** is the rate at which primary producers create organic material.
  - A **limiting nutrient** is a single nutrient that is scarce and therefore limits growth in an ecosystem.
  - In aquatic ecosystems, **nitrogen** and **phosphorus** are often limiting nutrients.
  - **Algal Bloom:** A sudden, rapid growth of algae caused by an influx of a limiting nutrient (e.g., from fertilizer runoff).

# S1M-3 4.1 Climate

## 4.1 Climate

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Oscar 9-1. Range: 2.2, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Weather vs. Climate**

  - **Weather**: The day-to-day condition of Earth's atmosphere at a particular time and place (e.g., "It's raining and 10°C today").
  - **Climate:** The average, year-after-year conditions of temperature and precipitation in a particular region (e.g., "Seattle has a temperate, rainy climate").
  - **Microclimate**: Climate conditions in a small area that differ from the surrounding areas (e.g., the sunny, dry side of a tree vs. the shady, moist side).

**Factors That Determine Global Climate**

**1. Solar Energy and the Greenhouse Effect**

  - The main force that shapes climate is solar energy.
  - The **Greenhouse Effec**t is a natural process where certain gases in the atmosphere (greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor) trap heat, much like glass in a greenhouse.
  - This trapped heat makes Earth warm enough to live on. An increase in these gases increases the warming effect.

**2. Latitude and Solar Energy**

  - The curvature of Earth causes the sun's rays to strike at different angles, creating three main climate zones:
  - **Polar Zones**: Receive the least intense, most indirect sunlight. Cold year-round.
  - **Temperate Zones**: Experience seasonal variations as Earth tilts toward or away from the sun.
  - **Tropical Zone**: Receives nearly direct, intense sunlight year-round. Generally warm.

**3. Heat Transport in the Biosphere**

  - The **unequal distribution** of heat drives winds and ocean currents, which transport heat and moisture around the planet.
  - **Winds**: Created by the rising of warm air and the sinking of cool air.
  - **Ocean Current**s: Warm currents carry heat from the tropics toward the poles; cold currents bring cold water from the poles back toward the equator. These currents strongly influence the climate of nearby landmasses.

**4.2 Niches and Community Interaction.**

**Niches and Habitats**

  - A **habitat** is the general place where an organism lives (its "address").
  - A **niche** is the full range of physical and biological conditions in which a species lives and the way the species obtains what it needs to survive and reproduce (its "profession" or "role").
  - This includes the **tolerance** (range of environmental conditions it can withstand), resources it uses, and how it interacts with other species.

**Community Interactions**

  - **Competition:** Occurs when organisms of the same or different species attempt to use the same limited ecological resource.
    - **Competitive Exclusion Principle:** No two species can occupy exactly the same niche in the same habitat at the same time. One will be better at competing and will eventually exclude the other.
    - Species often **divide resources** to reduce competition.
  - **Predation:** An interaction where one animal (the predator) captures and feeds on another animal (the prey).
  - **Herbivory:** An interaction where an animal (the herbivore) feeds on producers (plants).
- **Symbiosis**
  - Any relationship in which two species live closely together.
  - **Mutualism:** Both species benefit from the relationship (e.g., clownfish and sea anemone).
  - **Parasitism:** One organism lives on or inside another organism (the host) and harms it (e.g., tapeworms, ticks).
  - **Commensalism:** One organism benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (e.g., barnacles on a whale).
- **Keystone Species**
  - A single species that can have a dramatic and disproportionate effect on the structure of an entire community.
  - Example: Sea otters eat sea urchins. If otters are removed, urchin populations explode and destroy kelp forests, which collapses the habitat for many other species.

## 4.3 Succession

- **Ecological Succession** is a series of more-or-less predictable changes that occur in a community over time after a disturbance.
- **Primary Succession**
  - Occurs on surfaces where **no soil exists** (e.g., after a volcanic eruption or retreating glacier).
  - The first species to colonize are called **pioneer species** (e.g., lichens and mosses). They help break down rock and form soil.
- **Secondary Succession**
  - Occurs when a disturbance affects the community **without completely destroying the soil** (e.g., after a wildfire, hurricane, or farming).
  - Proceeds faster than primary succession because soil and seeds are already present.
- **Climax Communities**
  - A mature, stable community that was thought to be the end result of succession.
  - Modern ecology shows that climax communities are not always uniform or stable and can be a patchwork of different stages due to frequent disturbances.

## 4.4 Biomes

**Climate vs. Weather**

  - **Weather** is the day-to-day condition of Earth's atmosphere.
  - **Climate** refers to average conditions, including temperature and precipitation, over long periods.

**Factors That Affect Global Climate:**

  - **Solar Energy and the Greenhouse Effect:** The trapping of heat by certain gases in the atmosphere (CO₂, methane, water vapor).
  - **Latitude:** The curvature of Earth causes solar energy to strike at different angles, creating three main climate zones: **polar, temperate, and tropical.**
  - **Heat Transport:** Winds and ocean currents transport heat and moisture around the globe.

A **biome** is a complex of terrestrial communities that covers a large area and is characterized by certain soil, climate conditions, and specific groups of plants and animals.

**Major Biomes**

  - **Tropical Rain Forest:** Hot and wet year-round; greatest species diversity; nutrient-poor soil.
  - **Desert:** Less than 25 cm of rain per year; can be hot or cold; organisms adapted to conserve water.
  - **Temperate Grassland:** Seasonal precipitation; fertile soils; maintained by fire and grazing.
  - **Temperate Forest:** Cold winters and warm summers; deciduous trees.
  - **Boreal Forest (Taiga):** Dense coniferous forests; long cold winters, short mild summers.
  - **Tundra:** Characterized by **permafrost** (a layer of permanently frozen subsoil); very cold, dry, and windy; low-growing vegetation.

## 4.5 Aquatic Ecosystems

**Factors Affecting Aquatic Ecosystems:**

  - **Water Depth:** Determines amount of sunlight.
    - **Photic Zone:** Sunlit upper layer where photosynthesis can occur.
    - **Aphotic Zone:** Permanently dark layer below.
  - **Temperature, Currents, and Nutrient Availability.**

**Freshwater Ecosystems**

  - **Rivers and Streams:** Water flows in one direction; organisms adapted to current.
  - **Lakes and Ponds:** Still water; food webs based on plankton.
  - **Freshwater Wetlands** (Bogs, Marshes, Swamps): Water covers the soil or is present at the surface; highly productive; filter pollutants and prevent flooding.

**Estuaries**

  - A special wetland formed where a river meets the sea, containing a mixture of fresh and salt water.
  - **Extremely important** as spawning and nursery grounds for many ecologically and commercially important fish and shellfish.

**Marine Ecosystems**

  - **Intertidal Zone:** Exposed to air and sun at low tide, submerged at high tide; organisms must tolerate extreme changes.
  - **Coastal Ocean:** From low-tide mark to the edge of the continental shelf; includes highly productive **kelp forests** and **coral reefs**.
  - **Open Ocean:** The vast, deep ocean.
    - **Photic Zone:** Base of most oceanic food webs (phytoplankton).
    - **Aphotic Zone:** Includes the deep sea, where food webs are based on material falling from above or on **chemosynthesis** at hydrothermal vents.

## 3.3 Energy Flow in Ecosystems

Energy flows through an ecosystem in a one-way stream, from primary producers to consumers.

Food chain: A series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by eating and being eaten. Food web: A model representing the many interconnected food chains in which energy flows. much more complicated than a single simple chain because many animals eat more than one kind of food.

Photoplankton: primary producers that are a mixture of floating algae; autotroph Zooplankton: small, swimming animals, feed on marine algae; heterotroph

Pyramid of numbers: the relative number of individual organisms at each trophic level in an ecosystem.

Pyramid of Biomass: the relative amount of living matter at each trophic level. Biomass is the total amount of living tissue within a given trophic level.

-human activity

Matter: anything that takes up space and has

mass never created or destroyed.

Carbon on the earth:

Living organisms: carbon compounds in producers, consumers, decomposers

Atmospherere: CO2

Lithosphere: carbonate rocks (CaCO3), fossil fuels (oil, coal), natural gas (CH4) Hydrosphere: dissolved CO2

Events of the cycle: Photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossilization, combustion.

The Nitrogen Cycle

-All organisms require nitrogen to make amino acids and nucleic acids, which are used to build proteins and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).

Nitrogen fixation:

-The bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonia NH3

- A small amount of nitrogen gas is converted to usable forms by lightning called atmospheric nitrogen fixation.

- Other soil bacteria convert NH3/NH4+ into nitrates and nitrites that primary producers Nitrogen-fixing bacteria can use to make proteins and nucleic acids

Ammonification

- Decomposers breakdown organic nitrogen compounds in waste and dead organisms to release ammonium NH4+.

Denitrification

-Other soil bacteria convert nitrates, nitrites into nitrogen gas.

-Phosphorus forms a part of vital molecules such as DNA and RNA.

-Although phosphorus is of great biological importance, it is not abundant in the biosphere.

Phosphorus cycles between geological and biological systems.

-Geological: Weathering and erosion release phosphorus from rocks.

-Biological: Phosphorus is taken up by producers, then passed to consumers.

-Long-term: Uplift returns phosphorus to rocks.

Nutrient Limitation: If ample sunlight and water are available, the primary productivity of an ecosystem may be limited by the availability of nutrients.

In soil: Fertilizers mainly supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium for plant growth. Micronutrients like iron and manganese are needed in tiny quantities.

In water: in saltwater(ocean), nitrogen is the limiting nutrient. In freshwater(lakes, streams), phosphorus is the limiting nutrient.

## 4.1 Climates

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Constance 9(11). Editor: Jenny 9(7). Range: 3.1-4.5 + 2.2. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Weather is the day-to-day condition of Earth’s atmosphere.

Climate refers to average conditions over long periods and is defined by year-after-year patterns of temperature and precipitation.

Two regions can have the same climate but different weather.

-Climate is rarely uniform even within a region.

-Environmental conditions can vary over small distances, creating microclimates.

3 Factors that effect climate

1. Solar Energy and Greenhouse Effect

-Greenhouse effect: Sunlight hits Earth. Part of the energy turns into heat. Some heat is blocked by atmospheric gases. This greenhouse effect keeps Earth’s average temperature stable. -greenhouse gases: Carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor

-if greenhouse gas concentration rise, earth warms because they trap more heat.

2. Latitude and Solar Energy

Near the equator, solar energy is intense. Polar areas receive less intense solar energy

3. Heat Transport in the Biosphere

Wind:

-Warm air near the equator rises, spreads toward the poles and cools down.

-Cold air near the poles sinks and flows back along Earth’s surface.

-This movement of air creates wind and transports heat.

-If Earth did not rotate, each hemisphere would have only one large circulation cell. -Earth’s rotation causes winds to blow generally from west to east over the

temperate zones and from east to west over the tropics and the poles.

Ocean currents:

-Surface currents affect the weather and climate of nearby landmasses

-Deep ocean currents form when cold polar water sinks and moves along the seabed. The water rises in warmer areas, and this process is upwelling.

## 4.2 Niche and Environmental Interactions

Tolerance: the ability to survive and reproduce under a range of environmental circumstances. Every species has its own range of tolerance.

Habitat: place where an organism lives

Niche: The range of physical and biological conditions in which a species lives and the way species obtains what it needs to survive and reproduce. Niche describes the occupation or position that an organism has in its environment. Each species occupies a distinct niche Physical aspects of Niche：abiotic factors

Biological aspects of Niche: biotic factors

Resource: any necessity of life (water, nutrients, light, food, or space)

-Competition occurs when organisms attempt to use the same limited resource in the time and place. It can occur between members of the same species (infraspecific competition), or between members of different species (interspecific competition).

-No two species can occupy exactly the same niche in exactly the same habitat at exactly the same time. This is because if two species was to occupy the same niche, one species would beat the other species and exclude the other species.

-Species divide their limited resources to avoid competition.

-Competition shape community by: helping to determine the number and kinds of species in a community, determining the niche each species occupies, causing species to divide resources

Predator-Prey Relationship: Interaction where one animal captures and feeds on another animal. Predators affect the size of prey populations and determine the places prey can live and feed. Usually in a community, the amount of prey is greater then the amount of predators. Herbivore-Plant Relationships: interaction where one animal feeds on producers. Herbivores can affect the size and distribution of plant populations and can determine the places certain plants can survive and grow.

Keystone Species: species that play a large roll in an ecosystem.

Symbiotic Relationships: The close relationship that exists when two or more species live together.

Mutualism : (+/+) benefit each other (eg. The clownfish is immune to anemone stings. When threatened by a predator, clownfish seek shelter by snuggling deep into an anemone’s tentacles. Commensalism: (+/0) one benefits and another is neither helped nor harmed. (Eg. Barnacles attach to the head of the whale and feed on plankton wherever the whale swims. The barnacles don’t harm the whale).

Parasitism: (+/-) one organism lives inside or on another organism and harms it. (Eg.Tapeworms live in the intestines of mammals, where they absorb large amounts of their hosts’ food. Fleas,

ticks, lice, and the leech shown, live on the bodies of mammals and feed on their blood and skin).

## 4.3 Succession

Ecological succession: A series of predictable changes that occur in a community over time. Primary Succession: The establishment of a community in an area of exposed rock that does not have any topsoil. Usually occurs very slowly at first.

Pioneer species: the first organism to appear. It helps to: Fix nitrogen, break down rocks, add organic matter to soil. Secondary Succession: Succession occurs where existing communities are not completely destroyed by disturbances. Proceeds faster than pri mary succession.

## 4.4 Biomes

Tropical Rain Forest

-Abiotic: Hot and wet all year round. Thin, nutrient-poor soil, easy to erode. Heavy rainfall (≥2 m per year)

-Abiotic: Warm all year, clear wet and dry seasons, rich but easily eroded soil -Biotic: Deciduous trees drop leaves in dry season to save water, some plants have thick waxy leaves, animals may estivate or migrate for water

Tropical Grassland / Savanna / Shrubland

Temperate Forest

-Abiotic: Cool to moderate winters, warm summers; year-round rain, fertile humus-rich soil -Biotic: Mix of deciduous trees (lose leaves in winter) and conifers, many animals hibernate or migrate in cold months

Northwestern Coniferous Forest

-Abiotic: Mild temperature, heavy rain in fall/winter/spring, dry summer, rocky acidic soil -Biotic: Tall conifers (redwood, spruce), moss covers trees, animals use camouflage, browsers eat varied plants

Boreal Forest

-Abiotic: Long cold winters, short mild summers, moderate rain, high humidity, acidic, nutrient-poor soil

-Biotic: Conical evergreen conifers with needle leaves to reduce water loss, animals have thick insulation or migrate south for winter

Tundra

-Abiotic: Strong winds, low precipitation, short soggy summers, long dark cold winters, permafrost -Biotic: Low-growing plants (mosses, lichens), plants hug ground to avoid wind, some animals migrate, year-round species have adaptations to reduce heat loss

Other land areas:

# S1F-1 5.1 How Populations Grow

## 5.1 How Populations Grow

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Oscar 9(1). Editor: Karen 9(6). Range: 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Describing Populations**

- **Geographic** **Range:** The actual area inhabited by a population. Ranges can be tiny (bacteria in a pumpkin) or vast (cod in the Atlantic Ocean). Human activities (like transporting species) can dramatically alter a species' range.
- **Population Density:** The number of individuals per unit area (e.g., 100 deer per square kilometer). Different species in the same environment can have very different densities.
- **Distribution (Dispersion Patterns):** How individuals are spaced relative to each other.
  - **Random:** Unpredictable spacing; resources are uniformly distributed (e.g., wildflowers in a field).
  - **Uniform:** Evenly spaced; often due to territorial behavior or competition (e.g., penguins nesting).
  - **Clumped:** Grouped together; most common pattern, due to patchy resources, social behavior, or reproductive patterns (e.g., elephant herds).

**Growth Rate:** Determines if a population increases, decreases, or remains stable. A **positive growth rate** means births + Immigration exceed deaths + emigration. A **negative growth rate** means the opposite.

- **Age Structure:** The number or percentage of males and females in each age group of a population (e.g., pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive). **This is the most critical factor for predicting future population growth.** A population with many young individuals will likely grow rapidly.

**Factors That Change Population Size**

- **Birthrate (Natality):** The number of births in a given time period.
- **Death Rate (Mortality):** The number of deaths in a given time period.
- **Immigration:** The influx of new individuals from other areas.
- **Emigration:** The exit of individuals from a population.

**Exponential Growth (J-Curve)**

- **Definition:** Growth pattern where a population's **growth rate accelerates as size increases**, because a constant percentage multiplies an ever-larger base number.
- **Conditions:** Occurs only under **ideal, unlimited conditions**—unlimited resources, no predators, no disease.
- **Graph:** Produces a characteristic **J-shaped curve**. The slope gets steeper over time.
- **Examples in Nature:**
  - **Rapid Reproducers:** Bacteria dividing every 20 minutes.
  - **New/Invasive Species:** Hydrilla in Florida, gypsy moths in the U.S., rabbits in Australia. These species experience a "lag phase" followed by explosive growth in a new environment lacking natural limiting factors.

**Logistic Growth (S-Curve)**

- **Definition:** A more realistic growth model where population growth slows and eventually stops due to environmental resistance.
- **Phases:**
  - **Exponential Phase:** Initial rapid growth when resources are abundant.
  - **Transitional Phase:** Growth rate begins to slow as resources become limited and competition increases.
  - **Plateau Phase:** Population growth stops; birth rate ≈ death rate and/or immigration ≈ emigration.
- **Graph:** Produces a characteristic **S-shaped (sigmoid) curve**.
- **Carrying Capacity (K):** The **maximum population size that a particular environment can sustain indefinitely**. Represented by the flat line at the top of the S-curve. Populations fluctuate around K due to environmental variations.

## 5.2 Limits to Growth

**Limiting** **Factors**

- **Definition:** Any factor that restrains the growth of a population. **Collectively, limiting factors determine the carrying capacity of an environment.**
- **Categories:**
  - **Density-Dependent Factors:** Their effect **increases as population density increases**. They regulate population size around the carrying capacity.
  - **Density-Independent Factors:** Affect populations **regardless of their size or density**. They can cause sudden, drastic population crashes.

**Density-Dependent** **Limiting** **Factors**

- **Competition:** Individuals of the same (**intraspecific**) or different (**interspecific**) species compete for limited resources like food, water, space, mates, or sunlight. **Increased density intensifies competition**, leading to lower birth rates, higher death rates, or increased emigration.
- **Predation:** The predator-prey relationship creates cyclical population dynamics, as seen in the classic **Isle** **Royale wolf-moose** study. More prey supports more predators, which then reduce the prey population, leading to a decline in predators, and so on.
- **Herbivory:** Similar to predation; herbivore populations cycle with the availability of their plant food sources.
- **Parasitism and Disease:** **Spread more rapidly in dense populations** where hosts are in close contact. Example: Canine parvovirus in the Isle Royale wolf population.
- **Stress from Overcrowding:** High density can cause psychological stress (in animals), leading to hormonal changes, suppressed immune systems, decreased parental care, aggression, and lower reproduction rates.

**Density-Independent** **Limiting** **Factors**

- **Abiotic, physical factors** that strike affects all population.
- **Examples:** Severe weather (hurricanes, droughts, blizzards), wildfires, volcanic eruptions, pesticide application, and major habitat destruction (e.g., a landslide).
- **The Key Difference:** These factors can **cause a population crash, but they do not** **regulate** **a population around a carrying capacity.** The population may recover quickly or stay low.

**Controlling Invasive Species: A Key Application**

- Invasive species like **zebra** **mussels** or **hydrilla** grow exponentially because the **density-dependent limiting factors from their native habitat (specific predators, parasites, diseases) are absent.**
- Control efforts often try to re-establish these checks (e.g., introducing a natural predator like grass carp for hydrilla) or use artificial density-independent methods (herbicides, manual removal), which are often expensive and temporary.

## 5.3 Human Population Growth

**Historical Overview**

- **For most of history (< 1800s):** Very slow growth. **High birth rates** were offset by **very high death rates** (famine, disease, lack of medicine).
- **Industrial Revolution (~1800s) onward:** **Exponential growth** began. Advances in **agriculture, medicine, sanitation, and technology** caused a dramatic **drop in death rates**, while birth rates remained high. This is the fundamental cause of the modern population explosion.

**Patterns of Growth: Demography**

- **Demography:** The scientific study of human population statistics (births, deaths, age structure, etc.).
- **The Demographic Transition:** A model explaining the shift from high to low birth and death rates. **It is not a law, but an observed pattern in many developed nations.**
  - **Stage I (Pre-Industrial): High birth rate, High death rate.** Slow, unpredictable growth. (Most of human history).
  - **Stage II (Transitional): High birth rate, FALLING death rate.** **Rapid exponential growth.** This is where many developing countries were/still are.
  - **Stage III (Industrial): FALLING birth rate, Low death rate.** Population growth slows. Birth rates fall due to increased education, urbanization, lower child mortality, and greater status for women.
  - **Stage IV (Post-Industrial): Low birth rate, Low death rate.** Population stabilizes or even declines slightly.
- **Age-Structure Diagrams (Population Pyramids):**
  - **Wide base (many young):** Predicts rapid future growth (e.g., **Guatemala**).
  - **Nearly vertical sides:** Predicts slow, steady growth or stability (e.g., **United States**).
  - **Inverted pyramid (narrow base):** Predicts future population decline (e.g., Japan, some European nations).
- **Future Projections:** Global growth is slowing, but the population is still increasing. Nearly all future growth will occur in **developing countries**. The challenge of **Stage II** growth has profound implications for global resource use and environmental impact.
